title: Passengers recount terrifying attempted hijack of Dubai-to-Israel flight
summary: Passenger Ron Levi tells CBS News the attempted hijack of a Dubai-to-Israel flight was "the scariest thing possible."
story: Passenger accounts paint a chaotic and terrifying picture of the alleged attempted hijacking of FlyDubai Flight 1073 on Wednesday. The flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv was forced to make an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia, and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said one pilot stabbed his counterpart and tried to crash the Boeing 737 Max 8 aircraft.

"As they were approaching Israel, one of the pilots stabbed the other pilot, and apparently attempted to crash the plane with everyone on board," Netanyahu said in a video statement, lauding passengers he said had helped to "neutralize the pilot."
Israeli Defense Minister Israel Katz called it "an attempted jihadist terror attack."
"It was the most frightening experience we've ever had in our lives," passenger Ron Levi told CBS News on Wednesday.
Two U.S. officials told CBS News that four people with dual U.S.-Israeli citizenship were aboard the flight.
Here's what we know about how the suspected terror attack unfolded, based on accounts from Levi and other passengers.
"Worse than a free-fall"

"The flight was going well, we were two hours in," Levi told CBS News' Dov Lieber, speaking from Tabuk, Saudi Arabia, where the plane made its safe emergency landing, piloted by an off-duty flight crew member who happened to be on board.
"All of a sudden, what we thought was turbulence started," said Levi. It kept getting stronger, and "we realized it's not something regular."
"I would say much worse than a free-fall," he said, describing how the plane "started turning all sideways and going up and down in all different kinds of directions, for a pretty long time."
"It's very hard to even to estimate if this was 30 seconds or a minute or more than that … it was just the scariest thing possible."
Levi was sitting in a row of seats with his family, "just holding each other's hands and saying that we love them and just hoping for the best."
"And then shouting started from the front of the plane," he recalled. He saw some people near the front get up.
"Very stressful situation"

Passenger Adam Polo was in row 13, hugging his 6-year-old son while his wife was hugging their 3-year-old daughter. Polo told CBS News he "tried to be cool" for his children and told them, "We will be OK."

"The first couple of minutes was very terrifying; you just feel like you're going to crash, but even after the plane was stabilizing, there was more than an hour where we were in the air without the primary crew members," Polo said.
Polo said he couldn't see much from his seat, but after 15 minutes, he saw a passenger running out of the cockpit covered in blood.
"No one from the crew members told us what was happening," Polo said. "The only ones to give us information was the passengers who stood up with an act of bravery."
Polo, who lives in Israel and was vacationing in Thailand with his family, said everything happened so fast and it was a "very stressful situation."
"I'm a pretty cynical guy, I'm not getting excited easily, but I think it was one of the most exciting moments of my life when the plane touched the ground," Polo said.
"The co-pilot tried to murder the pilot"

Levi said he wasn't close enough to see what happened next, but several other passengers who spoke with Israeli media said one pilot had stabbed the other, details that were also repeated by Netanyahu.
"According to the initial information in our possession, the terrorist's intention was one thing: to crash the plane with all its passengers," said Katz, Israel's defense chief.

Netanyahu said he had spoken with an Israeli passenger who told him that, "somehow, he managed to break into the cockpit together with one of the crew members, and that together they neutralized the pilot who carried out the stabbing while he was attempting to sabotage the aircraft's systems."
Passenger Miryam Shira Ohayon said the plane was "pretty much out of control" when the stabbing took place, she believed somewhere over Jordan.

"The co-pilot tried to murder the pilot and basically carry out a suicide attack on the plane," she told reporters by speakerphone, held up by her mother who was waiting at Ben Gurion Airport near Tel Aviv. "It was really on the way to crashing, and it was simply the resourcefulness of many people who took control of the co-pilot and neutralized him."

Another passenger told The Jerusalem Post that intervening passengers shouted at two off-duty pilots at the back of the plane "to run and take control" of it, and one of them did so after the passengers managed to remove the attacker from the cockpit.
Netanyahu said the person who "managed to stabilize the aircraft" was "another aircrew member who was on the plane."

"All we heard in the back was shouting," said Levi. "We saw that some people were dealing with stuff, and it kept on going like that for, I think, about 10, 20 minutes until … the shakiness [of the plane] relaxed."
"Rumors started coming, and we realized that it wasn't just turbulence," he said. "It was something … a lot worse than that."
"They're heroes," he said of the people who intervened to stop the attacking pilot. "We owe them our lives."
Levi said he saw people covered in blood.
"They're here with us as well now," he told CBS News from the airport in Saudi Arabia. "These were the people I'm talking about who … jumped into the cockpit even and saved the situation."
According to Ohayon, a doctor and others on board helped treat the pilot for unspecified wounds.
"Other than the pilot, there were no injuries, but the bigger fear was really a crash, which is exactly what he was trying to do," she said.
"I just want to go home"
An Israeli security official told CBS News on Wednesday that Israel is investigating whether it was intended to be a Sept. 11-style terror attack, and whether the attacker was working alone.
The pilot was arrested and taken for questioning by Saudi authorities, Netanyahu said, adding that Israel was working to bring the passengers back to Israel safely.
"There's another FlyDubai plane here now," said Levi. "People are a bit reluctant to get on it, naturally. … We want to go home, but we want to do it in a safe way."
Asked how he was processing the incident, Levi replied: "Honestly, I'm not even starting. We're all shaking here … I have no idea. I just want to go home."
The flight landed safely in Tel Aviv around 8 p.m. local time Wednesday. Cheers and chants could be heard as the passengers disembarked.

During a recent interview on "Piers Morgan Uncensored," the 75-year-old musician reflected on the toll his career took on his relationships with his children and how it affected his three marriages.

"To some extent, I have to say I regret my marriages falling apart," he explained. "Sometimes I jumped. Well, one time I jumped, two times I was pushed. But I wouldn't have written it like that. "It was the 70s," he said. "That’s what was happening back then. People were just treating it like it was toothpaste, and you had to do it twice a day to stay healthy."

title: Chris Rock shreds 'woke 1.0' era, compares modern outrage to Salem witch hunts
summary: Chris Rock compares cancel culture to Salem witch hunts and the Old Testament, arguing wokeness also needs to come with a willingness to forgive.
story: Former Superman star says the industry is emerging from its 'woke era,' explains why filmmakers are fleeing California, and reveals what comes next
Chris Rock is getting candid about the importance of forgiveness in a world so quick to cancel others.

During a recent appearance on "The Daily" podcast, the 61-year-old comedian discussed his issues with "wokeness," saying that while advocating for marginalized people and giving them a voice is great, it needs to come with forgiveness.

"The problem with wokeness is we're in the Old Testament right now," he said. "And the Old Testament has no forgiveness. The Old Testament didn't work. So they had to write a remix called the New Testament."

Host David Marchese then asked if he thought there was "anything redeeming" that came out of the post-George Floyd era, which he referred to as "woke 1.0," since Democratic politicians now seem to be straying further from that ideology now.
Rock compared wokeness to the Salem witch trials. (Jemal Countess/WireImage)
SKILLET'S JOHN COOPER SAYS WOKE ACTIVISTS HAVE 'BIG HEARTS' BUT ARE 'HURTING THEMSELVES'
The "Grown Ups" star reiterated his position that "it's great to help those that need help," but noted the problem comes "when you institutionalize it."

"The Salem witch hunts. I'm sure the first three witches they caught were actually f- - -ing witches," he said. "But then you open up a witch office and now you've got to start lying. Now you've gotta f- - - ing make s- - - up because you've got overhead. You've got to justify the witch hunters f - - -ing pensions and s- - -."

He explained that just because he advocates for forgiveness, it "doesn't mean condoning abusive behavior. You can reprimand your friends," adding that holding them accountable is "also part of friendship."
"If you’re only friends with your friends when they’re good, they’re not your friends," he said.
Rock said part of friendship is holding each other accountable. (Leon Bennett/EveryStory2026/WireImage)

While he admits there is room for improvement when it comes to cancel culture and wokeness, he noted he is "glad that all of this stuff happened," as it allowed for certain voices to be heard which otherwise may not have been.
Kaivan Shroff — a former Hillary Clinton campaign staffer – disagreed with Rock, telling Fox News Digital the comedian "is oversimplifying this in a way that is pretty self-serving."

title: Michael Douglas confirms secret affair with Kathleen Turner on 'Romancing the Stone' set
summary: Michael Douglas reveals in his memoir, "One Helluva Ride," that he and Kathleen Turner kept their "Romancing the Stone" affair secret for 40 years.
story: Fox News Flash top entertainment and celebrity headlines are here.
Michael Douglas is confirming a rumor that has followed him around for decades.

In an excerpt from his upcoming memoir, "One Helluva Ride," the 82-year-old actor revealed he and Kathleen Turner had an affair while filming "Romancing the Stone," a rumor they denied for over 40 years.

"Kathleen was smart, funny, and sexy with a deep, sultry voice that became her signature," he wrote in an excerpt obtained by People. "I instantly liked her, and we were immediately attracted to each other."
He said, although he was married to Diandra Luker at the time, "things at home were in a bad place" and both he and Luker "were both having extramarital affairs."
MICHAEL DOUGLAS' ACADEMY AWARD-WINNING ROLE IN ‘WALL STREET’ WAS FIRST OFFERED TO THESE TWO A-LIST ACTORS
Douglas admitted he and Turner had an affair while filming "Romancing the Stone." (20th Century Fox/Getty Images)

Douglas wrote that he left home to film the 1984 movie "still technically married, but separated," and that while audiences were "certain for years that we were in a relationship together" while making the movie, they denied it, even through the making of the sequel and years later when they reunited on "The Kominsky Method."
The two told the public that while they "had amazing chemistry" and were "both tempted," they never acted on their feelings.

"The truth is that during the production of Romancing the Stone, Kathleen and I fell hard for each other and began a relationship," he wrote. "It wasn’t a fly-by night affair; it grew naturally from how closely we were working together, how much pressure we were under, how much we respected and cared for one another, and how attracted we were to each other. Like every other guy in the world at the time, I was knocked sideways by Kathleen."
He noted that the two of them kept their affair a secret for 40 years to protect Luker and their son, Cameron.

"There were no cameras in elevators, no assistants using cell phones to take pictures," he said. "As Jack and Joan were falling in love, Kathleen and I were keeping the chemistry alive."
Douglas and Turner were falling in love as their characters were doing the same on screen. (Sunset Boulevard/Corbis via Getty Images)

title: Prince William, Kate Middleton’s secret nicknames exposed as former staffer reveals palace WhatsApp habits
summary: Royal family WhatsApp nicknames exposed by a former staffer, from Prince William's "Bobcat" to Prince Harry's "Baz" and other secret aliases.
story: Royal broadcaster Ian Pelham Turner shares the private nicknames reportedly used by Kate Middleton, Prince William, King Charles and other royals.
Behind palace doors, it's apparently less "Your Royal Highness" and more "Bobcat."

A former royal staffer is pulling back the curtain on Prince William and Kate Middleton's reported WhatsApp nicknames. Jack Stooks, who worked for King Charles for 21 years as a gardener at Highgrove, shared a rare glimpse into how members of the royal family reportedly identified one another on the messaging app.
"I remember Princes William and Harry always had the latest phones," Stooks explained to GB News.
"They actually gave their numbers out to staff so we could contact them about logistical things. They also had our numbers, and they would just WhatsApp us if they needed anything.
PRINCE WILLIAM AND KATE MIDDLETON’S ‘GENUINE LOVE STORY' IS BUILT ON BEING A 'VERY NORMAL FAMILY': AUTHOR

Prince William, Prince of Wales, and Catherine, Princess of Wales, are given a tour by Jamie Jones Buchanan, CEO of the Leeds Rhinos during a visit to AMT Headingley Stadium, the home of the Leeds Rhinos rugby team, Sept. 29, 2026 in Leeds, England.  (James Glossop/WPA Pool/Getty Images)

"We couldn't have them saved under their real names, so they had nicknames instead," said Stooks. "William was 'Bobcat', Harry was ‘Baz,’ and when Catherine joined the family, she became ‘Mrs. Bobcat.’"
Stooks told Fox News Digital on behalf of OLBG that only a limited number of staff were given the royals' phone numbers, which had to be kept a closely guarded secret.
Prince William, Prince of Wales, and Catherine, Princess of Wales, at the DMMI Royal Charity Polo Cup 2026 in Windsor, England, July 10, 2026. (Max Mumby/Indigo/Getty Images)

"We had the family under different names, so that if anyone's phone was taken, the number could be differentiated," he explained. "That way, no one knew which number was which. They all change their numbers regularly, so I don't have any of their phone numbers now."
WATCH: ROYAL FAMILY'S CHEEKY NICKNAMES FOR EACH OTHER REVEALED

"The nickname I gave to Harry on my phone was ‘Baz,’" Stooks shared. "He was always called ‘Baz’ by his friends, so I just took that. From memory, William was ‘Wombat,’ again because that is what his friends called him."
Prince William drives a tractor alongside Catherine, Princess of Wales, during cleanup activities at Ettrick Bay on the Isle of Bute, Scotland, Sept. 17, 2026. (Samir Hussein/WireImage)
Fox News Digital reached out to Buckingham Palace and Kensington Palace for comment.
Stooks told GB News members of the royal family "are big WhatsApp users."

Prince William, Prince of Wales, meets well-wishers during a visit to the Millennium Powerhouse, a multiservice youth hub in the Moss Side neighborhood of Manchester, England, Nov. 16, 2023. (Getty Images)

"He may have a lot of privilege, but William was never one to demand something from staff," Stooks told the outlet. "He was really polite. He would always check how busy I was before asking me to do errands for him. And whenever I said I would do something for William, he would always reply, 'You're a legend.'

"They have groups with their friends, and there is also a family group with the royal cousins, including Prince William, Zara Tindall, Peter Phillips and the York sisters," he continued. "They're very much like any other family when it comes to keeping in touch through their phones."
Prince William, Prince of Wales, and Catherine, Princess of Wales, arrive for a visit to Southport Community Centre in Southport, England, Oct. 10, 2024. (Getty Images)

Several royal experts told Fox News Digital that members of the royal family have long used nicknames. Some are terms of affection, while others have reportedly been used as aliases for privacy or security.

Prince William, Prince of Wales, known as the Duke of Rothesay, and Catherine, Princess of Wales, known as the Duchess of Rothesay when in Scotland, smile to well-wishers as they arrive for a visit to Aros Hall, a local community hub on April 29, 2025, in Tobermory, Scotland. (Chris Jackson/Getty Images)
"When they had a security issue, William and Kate are known as Danny Collins and Daphne Clark, DC," royal broadcaster Ian Pelham Turner told Fox News Digital.

"In other words, Duke and Duchess of Cambridge," he said, referring to the Prince and Princess of Wales. "The late queen was always known as Sharon, believe it or not, just for the simple S, which stood for sovereign.

Prince William, Prince of Wales, smiles as he rides in a boat during a tour of the Guapimirim mangrove area in Guanabara Bay, managed by the Chico Mendes Institute for Biodiversity Conservation, on Nov. 4, 2025, in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil. (Aaron Chown-Pool/Getty Images)

"King Charles and Queen Camilla, do they call themselves that? No," said Turner. "They call themselves Fred and Gladys. Why? Because in the 1950s and 1960s, Prince Charles used to listen to a radio show each week called 'The Goon Show,' which was a comedy show where Fred and Gladys were called. When he started a romance with Queen Camilla, the joke started as well. That's where Fred and Gladys first started.
King Charles and Queen Camilla attend the traditional Easter Sunday service at St. George's Chapel April 9, 2023, in Windsor. (Max Mumby/Indigo/Getty Images)
"And then you would think, ‘Why on earth would the queen, Elizabeth that is, be called any other nickname other than Your Majesty?’" he said. "Prince Philip used to call the queen Cabbage."
British broadcaster Helena Chard told Fox News Digital the name derived from the French "mon petit chou," or "my little cabbage."
Queen Elizabeth II and Prince Philip, the Duke of Edinburgh, revisit Broadlands in Hampshire to mark their Diamond Wedding Anniversary on Nov. 20, 2007. (Tim Graham/Getty Images)
"I believe he also affectionately called her sausage," Chard added.

Britain's King Charles III and Queen Camilla wave to crowds from the balcony of Buckingham Palace during Trooping The Colour in London on June 13, 2026. (Kirsty Wigglesworth/AP)
"When Prince William, as a little boy, fell at Buckingham Palace, he was overheard by a guest crying out, 'Gary! Gary!’" said British royals expert Hilary Fordwich.

Queen Elizabeth sits with Prince William and Prince Harry in the royal box at Guards Polo Club, Smiths Lawn, Windsor. (Tim Graham Photo Library via Getty Images)
Several royal experts noted that, at university, William was known as "Steve" in an attempt to fly under the radar.

One of the royal family's best-known nicknames is "Lilibet." Then-Princess Elizabeth struggled to pronounce her own name as a toddler, and her grandfather, King George V, reportedly imitated her pronunciation. Her husband, Prince Philip, also affectionately called her "Lilibet," and the name was later chosen by Prince Harry and Meghan Markle for their daughter, Princess Lilibet.
But not all royal nicknames were affectionate.
Queen Elizabeth II and Prince Harry attend the annual Chelsea Flower Show at Royal Hospital Chelsea on May 18, 2015, in London, England. (Julian Simmonds/WPA Pool /Getty Images)
"Courtiers have long referred to Prince Harry and the former Prince Andrew, as the 'Dukes of Hazard,' which needs no explanation," said Fordwich.

Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor and his ex-wife, Sarah Ferguson, attend the funeral of Katharine, Duchess of Kent, at Westminster Cathedral on Sept. 16, 2025, in London, England. (Mark Cuthbert/UK Press via Getty Images)

"When Kate is getting a little bit upset with William in any way, she starts using the names of 'Baldy' and ‘Big Willy,'" Turner alleged, a claim previously made by author Tom Quinn. A Kensington Palace spokesperson previously told Fox News Digital that the palace doesn't comment on books.
King Charles has reportedly used other terms of affection for Queen Camilla.
Queen Camilla hosts a reception at Clarence House in London, England, to mark 40 years of the Royal Osteoporosis Society on July 15, 2026. (Aaron Chown/WPA Pool/Getty Images)
"Back in 2022, the king was heard at an event referring to Camilla as 'Mehbooba,' the Urdu word for 'my beloved,'" said Fordwich.
King Charles III and Queen Camilla attend a service at Crathie Kirk Church on Aug. 23, 2026, in Crathie, Aberdeenshire. (Peter Summers/Getty Images)
Charles has publicly used the term for Camilla. While still Prince of Wales, he referred to her as "my mehbooba" during a British Asian Trust speech.

"Princess Diana's family always referred to her as 'Dutch,' short for 'Duchess.' She wasn't an actual duchess, but her family gave it to her as she had always behaved that way as a young girl. Her nickname for her brother, Charles Spencer, was 'Carlos,'" Fordwich said.
Charles Spencer, Princess Diana's brother, attends a reception celebrating the "Diana: A Celebration" exhibit at the National Constitution Center in Philadelphia on Oct. 1, 2009. (Getty Images)

Charles Spencer has also spoken about the siblings' nicknames. In a September interview, he said their stepfather began calling Diana "the Duchess" because she had a "very refined air," which the family shortened to "Dutch." Spencer also said Diana called him "Carlos."
Diana, Princess of Wales, died in 1997. She was 36. (Tim Graham Photo Library via Getty Images)
Stooks told GB News that these days, it would be difficult to know what name the king uses, if any, on WhatsApp.

Prince George of Wales and King Charles III watch an RAF flypast from the balcony of Buckingham Palace following the coronation of King Charles III and Queen Camilla at Westminster Abbey on May 6, 2023, in London. (Max Mumby/Indigo/Getty Images)

"The king didn't really use technology at all when I worked there," he said. "He used to have a very old-fashioned, basic mobile phone, but he never used it. I remember William and Harry trying to get him to keep up to date with it. They were always encouraging him to use his phone, but he wasn't interested. He wasn't a fan at all."

title: EXCLUSIVE: Michael McDonald’s long-lost son reveals stunning moment he discovered famous father after 58 years
summary: A St. Louis man adopted through Catholic Charities nearly 60 years ago learned his biological father is Doobie Brothers singer Michael McDonald.
story: Michael Goessling tells Fox News Digital how a mysterious call with a musician named ‘Mike’ led to an unbelievable realization with a quick internet search.

EXCLUSIVE: Michael Goessling always knew he was adopted. But what he did not know for nearly 58 years was that his biological father had one of the most recognizable and beloved voices in American music.

The St. Louis man learned recently that his father is five-time Grammy winner and Doobie Brothers singer Michael McDonald, a musician Goessling had admired since childhood and had unknowingly paid to see perform twice as a young man.

But even after receiving the letter that began it all, meeting his biological mother and learning his biological father was a mysterious musician named "Mike," Goessling still had no idea who was waiting on the other end of the phone.
RITA WILSON LEARNED ABOUT FATHER’S TRAGIC PAST, SECRET FAMILY IN BULGARIA ON TV SHOW
Michael Goessling, right, spoke with Fox News Digital about discovering at age 58 that Michael McDonald was his biological father. (Courtesy of Michael Goessling)
The answer finally came during their first conversation, when "Mike" mentioned he was touring and would be stopping in St. Louis on Sept. 4 at a venue he believed was called "Hollywood."

Goessling thought of the Hollywood Casino Amphitheater and, puzzled that his biological father was apparently still a touring musician at his age, began searching the venue's concert schedule as the two men spoke.
The Doobie Brothers were playing in concert Sept. 4.
Suddenly, the pieces began falling into place: "Mike." Musician. That unmistakable voice.
"Are you Michael McDonald?" Goessling finally asked.
McDonald chuckled. "Yep, afraid so."
"Oh my gosh, this is getting crazier by the second," Goessling recalled saying. "I can't even, I can't get my head around this. This is too much."
"I know," McDonald replied. "Take a minute."
"I thought I was being punked for a second," Goessling told Fox News Digital. "It's like, 'No, this can't be real. This is impossible. What is going on here?'"
More than a year later, he said the discovery can still feel unreal.
NEW CALIFORNIA LAW EXPANDS DNA TOOLS FOR MISSING PERSONS INVESTIGATIONS
Michael Goessling credits his adoptive parents, Paul and Kay Goessling, with giving him a "charmed" childhood. (Courtesy of Michael Goessling)
"I still wake up sometimes and my first thought is, ‘Oh my gosh, that was a crazy dream,’ only to realize that here we are."

The extraordinary phone call came just days after a letter ended a mystery stretching back to Goessling's birth. On May 6, 2025, an attorney representing his biological mother contacted Goessling to explain that she believed he was the son she had placed for adoption through Catholic Charities nearly 58 years earlier.
Goessling had always known he was adopted, but the adoption was closed. He knew nothing about his biological parents, and they knew virtually nothing about the life he had gone on to live.

His biological mother, he learned, had spent roughly 30 to 35 years searching for him. Both biological parents hoped he might be willing to communicate, Goessling recalled, but above all, they wanted to know that he was well.
"It was a wonderful surprise but quite a shock," he said. "It felt like a tsunami hit me."
Goessling called his biological mother that evening. Although he had never actively searched for his biological parents, he had long hoped he might someday have the opportunity to thank them.

"I just want you to hear from me that I got nothing but love for you," he recalled telling her. "This is such an amazing gift, that I get to thank you personally. … They were always heroes in my story," he said.
CUT OFF BY YOUR ADULT CHILD? PSYCHOLOGY RESEARCHER REVEALS WHAT PARENTS SHOULD DO NEXT
Michael Goessling said people compared his appearance to Michael McDonald years before he discovered the singer was his biological father. (Courtesy of Michael Goessling)
Their first conversation lasted about 90 minutes. Goessling eventually proposed meeting for lunch that Friday, prompting his biological mother to remind him that Friday was his birthday.
"Yeah, yeah. You've waited long enough. I think I've waited enough," he recalled replying. "Let's meet on my birthday, 58 years to the day."

After a three-hour lunch and nearly six decades apart, Goessling learned there was someone else anxious to speak with him. His biological father had deliberately remained in the background so mother and son could have their reunion first.

"He really wanted the mother-son thing to happen first, which is just true to his character," Goessling said. "He thought that was very important, and he wanted to take a back seat so that could happen."
Before father and son connected, McDonald left Goessling a voicemail. That unmistakable voice immediately struck him.
"Whoa, what a voice," Goessling recalled telling his biological mother.
"Yeah, he gets that a lot," she replied with a chuckle.
The voice seemed strangely familiar, but Goessling still didn't make the connection. When the two men finally spoke, he began by telling McDonald what he had already told his biological mother.
"Thank you for giving me a shot in this world," Goessling recalled saying. "I've had a charmed life. And it all started with you guys."
Then he asked what his biological father did for a living.
"I'm a musician," McDonald told him.

Goessling, a lifelong music obsessive who once worked in the music business, thought that was terrific. It wasn't until the conversation turned to McDonald's upcoming tour stop that he finally put it together.
The revelation contained another coincidence almost too remarkable to invent; Goessling was already a huge fan.

The Doobie Brothers had been among his favorite bands since childhood, alongside The Who and Journey. He vividly remembers first hearing "Takin' It to the Streets" after McDonald joined the group and insisting to the person playing it that there had been some mistake.
"I know the Doobie Brothers and that is not the Doobie Brothers," Goessling remembered declaring as a child.
He soon learned about the band's new singer and became a McDonald fan, too. He remained one.

In fact, Goessling had already watched his biological father perform in concert twice, once in the 1980s, and again in the early 1990s, without ever imagining that the man onstage was the father whose identity he did not know.
When Fox News Digital pointed out that meant he had actually paid twice to see his own father perform, Goessling laughed.
"I should get reimbursed for that."

There were other clues hiding in plain sight. After Goessling grew out his hair and white beard during the COVID-19 pandemic, people began telling him they liked the "Michael McDonald thing" he had going on.
"Little did I know, five years later that that would resonate even so true," he said.

After the families met, the similarities became even harder to miss. During a visit with McDonald, Goessling said McDonald's wife, Amy, and his newfound half-sister would watch him do or say something and suddenly burst out laughing.
Michael McDonald of The Doobie Brothers in 2021. McDonald has a new memoir titled, "What a Fool Believes."  (Chris Pizzello/AP Photo, File)

"Your dad does the exact same thing," they would tell him. "They couldn't take their eyes off me," Goessling said. "They're waiting to see what I would do or say next because there was so many just natural similarities."
Yet, for Goessling, the remarkable celebrity connection is not the part of his story that matters most.

Learning where he came from also meant finally understanding what his biological parents had faced nearly six decades earlier, when they were just two 14-year-old eighth-graders confronting a pregnancy that would change all three of their lives.

According to Goessling, the teenagers' initial reaction was that they would marry, raise their baby and rely on their families to help them. Their parents concluded they were simply too young at the time.
"They were just far too young to be married and to have a child," Goessling said.
Their families ultimately determined that adoption would be best, he said, although relinquishing their son had not been his biological parents' first choice.
Nearly six decades later, Goessling sees what happened through the lens of both gratitude and faith.
"Mike, I mean, he wasn't Michael McDonald [then]. He was Mike from the neighborhood," he said, imagining how differently life could have been had two 14-year-olds attempted to raise a child together.
Patrick Simmons, left, Tom Johnston, John McFee, Marc Russo, Michael McDonald and Ed Toth of The Doobie Brothers perform onstage in Pacific Palisades, Calif. (Kevin Mazur/Getty Images for BC, File)

"I have to believe that it all worked out as it was supposed to because, certainly, when I see us all now together, it's just the greatest joy," Goessling said. "I think this was the plan. And I think it was a beautiful plan."

That plan, as Goessling sees it, led him to Paul and Kay Goessling. He grew up in a family of four children. Three were adopted before, against the odds, Kay became pregnant with their youngest daughter, Linda.
Goessling describes his childhood as "charmed" and said he could not have chosen better parents himself.
"If I could go back and pick two folks, I would pick them and do it all over again," he said. "They were just the most wonderful blessing in my life."
His father, Paul, died shortly before Christmas 2024 after a long battle with Parkinson's disease, and Goessling said the two were extremely close. Six months later, another father entered his life.
"After losing my father, I get a letter, and Mike pops up," Goessling said. "Another father enters my life, my world."
Kay's reaction to the discovery was immediate. When Goessling showed her the letter, he said his mother began crying and declared what had happened "a miracle."
Michael Goessling with his adoptive father, Paul Goessling. (Courtesy of Michael Goessling)
Michael Goessling, here with his siblings many decades ago, credits his adoptive parents with giving him a "charmed" childhood. (Courtesy of Michael Goessling)
She asked whether he had met his biological mother, and he had.
"Oh my God, go get her," Goessling recalled Kay saying. "I have to meet her. I've got a million questions. What's she like? I gotta give her a big hug."
Goessling said his mother has embraced his biological family from the beginning, and the once-separate branches of his family came together with surprising ease.
"Everybody's in love with everybody," he said.
Father and son now speak frequently and text "all the time," according to Goessling.
And while the identity of his biological father is what thrust his story into the spotlight, Goessling hopes the attention gives him an opportunity to talk about adoption as a blessing.

A practicing Catholic who was raised in the faith and adopted through Catholic Charities, Goessling said his parents taught him from childhood to understand his adoption not as evidence that he had been unwanted, but as evidence that he was deeply loved.
Michael McDonald and Michael Goessling with family. (Courtesy of Michael Goessling)
Even before he was old enough to fully understand what adoption meant, he knew how his parents viewed it.
"It was a miracle," he said. "It was the greatest thing. It was a gift from God."
Only when Goessling grew old enough to understand where babies came from, he said, did he fully appreciate the significance of the decisions that had been made before his birth.

"Obviously, we all know there are choices in this world, and I am so grateful and fortunate for the choices they made on my behalf," he said. "Adoption has been absolutely nothing but a blessing for me. … I celebrate adoption and I always have. It's always been a big part of my life story."
Now, nearly six decades later, Goessling has been able to thank the biological parents he once could only imagine, and discovered that they had spent those same decades wondering about him.
He hopes the unlikely circumstances that brought attention to his family can help "elevate" the conversation surrounding adoption.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
"I want this to elevate the narrative, the adoption narrative," he said. "I want that adoption gets celebrated more in this country. If my crazy story can be true, Lord knows anything is possible."
And if Michael McDonald is watching? Goessling doesn't need an interview to deliver the message. He said father and son already talk regularly.
"I just tell him that I love him, and I tell him thank you for everything," he said.
After 58 years, the man who says he never felt deprived of a family has somehow ended up with an even larger one.
"My cup overflows," Goessling said.

title: 'Piano Man' Billy Joel's prized motorcycle collection hits the auction block
summary: Billy Joel's prized motorcycle collection of over 70 lots hits the auction block at Retromobile New York, featuring Ducati, Triumph and more.
story: Gooding Christie's founder David Gooding told Fox News Digital that Billy Joel is a "genuine enthusiast" who loves all kinds of motorcycles.
Billy Joel may be right, or he may be crazy as his prized motorcycle collection hits the auction block in the Big Apple.
More than 70 lots from the Piano Man's personal collection will be offered without reserve during Gooding Christie's inaugural auction at Retromobile New York next month.

Joel, 77, "is a genuine enthusiast who loves all sorts of motorcycles," Gooding Christie's founder, David Gooding, exclusively told Fox News Digital of the array of two-wheelers going up for sale, which includes "older bikes, bikes with side cars ... a mixture of everything."
BILLY JOEL SAYS LOUD ROCK CONCERTS DAMAGED HIS NERVES, LED TO HIS BRAIN SURGERY AND NPH DIAGNOSIS
The "Piano Man" is an avid motorcycle enthusiast and will auction off over 70 items. (Billy Joel archives)
"The exciting thing is all the motorcycles are being sold without reserve," Gooding said, meaning the auction will be sold to the highest bidder regardless of the final price.
BILLY JOEL SAYS AGING MUSICIANS WHO KEEP MAKING RECORDS PAST THEIR PRIME 'DILUTE THEIR LEGACY'

"And, a portion of the proceeds are going to benefit the Joel Foundation, which is a wonderful charity. It's a great charity that supports non-profit music education, public women's health ... there's some great initiatives that it supports."
The collection includes a number of his most cherished motorcycles, including Ducati, BMW, Moto Guzzi, Harley-Davidson, Yamaha, Triumph, Honda, Kawasaki, and more.
Joel's 1975 Ducati 750 Sport is up for auction through the Gooding Christie's sale. (Mike Maez, Gooding & Company, LLC.)

"One of the stars of the sale is a 1978 Triumph T140 Bonneville that was gifted to Billy Joel by Madison Square Garden to commemorate 150 sold out shows," Gooding said of the bike, which is expected to retrieve anywhere from $10,000 - $15,000.
"He still holds the record for the most sold out show of anyone ever at Madison Square Garden. And this bike is painted with a keyboard on the tank. It's really, really a special, special item."

The custom-painted motorcycle was commissioned especially for Joel, and is accompanied by a matching helmet listing every single show and year he played at Madison Square Garden, according to Gooding.

Among the most captivating motorcycles in the collection is a 1978 Triumph T140 Bonneville gifted to Mr. Joel by Madison Square Garden on the occasion of his 150th sold-out show at the world-famous venue. (Mike Maez, Gooding & Company, LLC.)

The collection also includes an iconic 1982 Ducati 900 Mike Hailwood Replica, which is estimated between $15,000-$25,000, marketed by Ducati to commemorate the motorcycle that Mike Hailwood rode to his legendary comeback victory at the 1978 Isle of Man.

A restored 1975 Ducati 750 Sport is estimated at $25,000 - $35,000 without reserve, and is "one of the most beautiful motorcycles ever conceived," according to the auction house.
Motorcycles from the auction – which is slated for Nov. 20-21 – will be on display at the Javits Center in New York.
Gooding Christie’s announced the world-famous Billy Joel Motorcycle Collection as a leading consignment for its upcoming inaugural sale at the Javits Center in New York City. (Billy Joel Archives)
Billy Joel has been collecting motorcycles for decades. (Larry Busacca/Getty Images)

"The great thing about this collection is it's certainly going to appeal to Billy Joel's fan base, but I also believe there are many people that are going to just be very passionate about motorcycles themselves," Gooding said.
"So we've got this sort of dual pool of interested buyers because the bikes in and of themselves are really important and valuable and exciting, and then you've got the Billy Joel component."

"I’ve always been drawn to bikes built by people who cared about getting every detail right," Joel said in a statement shared through Gooding Christie's. "I’ve loved building this collection. Now it’s someone else’s turn to hit the road."

The "Uptown Girl" singer underwent brain surgery after revealing his normal pressure hydrocephalus (NPH) diagnosis in May 2025. NPH affects his vision, hearing and balance, according to a statement Joel released on social media at the time.
Billy Joel announced his normal pressure hydrocephalus (NPH) diagnosis in May 2025. (Myrna M. Suarez/Getty Images)
During a recent appearance on his self-titled SiriusXM show, "The Billy Joel Channel," the legendary singer said doctors told him that his rock 'n' roll lifestyle caused damage to his brain nerves.

At the time of the announcement, Joel was forced to cancel a number of shows and said his condition had been "exacerbated by recent concert performances, leading to problems with hearing, vision and balance."

NPH is a condition that happens when cerebrospinal fluid builds up inside the skull and presses on the brain. This condition is most likely to occur in people over age 65. Treating this condition involves surgery to implant a shunt to drain excess fluid from the inside of the skull, according to the Cleveland Clinic.

title: Johnny Depp's return in 'Ebenezer' divides fans as new trailer sparks debate
summary: Johnny Depp's transformation as Ebenezer Scrooge in the new "Ebenezer" trailer sparked debate over its "think again" tagline and revisionist marketing.
story: FOX Nation host Nancy Grace reacts to officials finding the remains of a missing Colorado mom and previews her exclusive interview with Jonny Depp’s attorney Camille Vasquez at CrimeCon 2023, streaming now on FOX Nation.
Johnny Depp is back in action – and his latest transformation quickly stirred up a spirited reaction.

The actor’s turn as Ebenezer Scrooge in the new "Ebenezer" trailer released Thursday earned enthusiastic praise from fans, while the film’s suggestion that audiences should "think again" about the classic story left others scratching their heads.

Johnny Depp transformed into Scrooge for the upcoming film "Ebenezer." (Daniel Knighton/Getty Images for Paramount Pictures)

"So many have done this story and I still will watch it."

title: Gordon Ramsay admits real reason he was crying while walking daughter down the aisle
summary: Gordon Ramsay reveals feeling "second best" after walking Holly Ramsay down the aisle and jokes about what really made him cry at the wedding.
story: "Knife Edge: Chasing Michelin Stars" executive producer Gordon Ramsay opens up about why he really became emotional while giving away his daughter Holly at her wedding.
Gordon Ramsay opened up about the bittersweet experience of giving away his daughter, Holly Ramsay, at her wedding.

Holly, 26, married Olympic swimmer Adam Peaty, 31, in December 2025 after the couple announced their engagement in 2024. The 59-year-old celebrity chef shares Holly, her twin brother Jack, daughters Megan, 28, and Matilda, 24, and sons Oscar, 7, and Jesse, 2, with his wife, Tana Ramsay, 52, whom he married in 1996.

During a recent interview with Fox News Digital, Ramsay, who is starring in season two of Apple TV's "Knife Edge: Chasing Michelin Stars," reflected on the close bonds that he shares with his three daughters and explained why he was left feeling "second best" after he walked Holly down the aisle.
GORDON RAMSAY SAYS ‘THE MOST IMPORTANT THING’ HE TAUGHT HIS SIX KIDS HAD NOTHING TO DO WITH COOKING

Gordon Ramsay revealed the real reason that he was crying while walking his daughter Holly down the aisle during her wedding last year. (Grant Buchanan/Dave Benett/Getty Images; Ben Birchall/PA Images via Getty Images)

"You grow up with these gorgeous girls and you teach them. I said to them, from an early age, they must have been 7 or 8 years of age, ‘The earlier you tell me, the more I can f---ing do," he recalled.

"They ignore you for two or three years," Ramsay continued. "But when they get to 11 or 12, ‘Hey daddy, you know what he said to me? The earlier you told me, the more you can do, I have a problem. Can I talk to you about it?’"
KELLY RIPA, MARK CONSUELOS SHARE BLUNT ADVICE FOR COUPLES PLANNING A BIG WEDDING

"Bang, then we're in,'" he added with a smile. "Then you're like that, you're sort of the BFF, right? Then you're a cool f---ing dad, then you're perfect. But when you walk them down the aisle, and you're minutes away from not being the number one guy in their life, and you're handing them over, man, that hits. That absolutely hits."
"So you have to understand that that relationship with your daughter is borrowed time before there's another man in their lives. Another partner in their life, that you become second best."

The "Hell's Kitchen" star noted that as a father of six, he will have to experience those moments multiple times in the future.

Ramsay quipped that his tears dried up once he realized that the flowers could be repurposed for a good cause.

Though Holly is the first of Ramsay's six children to walk down the aisle, he will soon have to give another daughter away. In an August appearance on "Live with Kelly and Mark," he revealed that Megan was engaged.

title: Sylvester Stallone showered in his clothes to survive before ‘Rocky’ fame
summary: Sylvester Stallone's memoir "The Steps" reveals how he survived on raw eggs and cottage cheese in a tiny New York City apartment before "Rocky" fame.
story: Sylvester Stallone joins Fox & Friends to discuss his new memoir, The Steps, opening up about his difficult upbringing, the lessons it taught him as a father and the personal experiences that inspired Rocky.

Before Sylvester Stallone became one of Hollywood's biggest stars, he had just $60 to his name — with $43.60 already set aside for rent. But even as he struggled to make ends meet in New York City, the future "Rocky" icon refused to give up on his dream.
In his new memoir, "The Steps," Stallone recounts the years before fame, including his arrival in New York City in 1969, determined to become an actor despite poverty, rejection and uncertainty.
The 80-year-old told Fox News Digital that even in his darkest moments, he held on to the belief that his life would eventually change for the better.
SYLVESTER STALLONE'S ADVICE TO THOSE WHO ARE STRUGGLING 50 YEARS AFTER 'ROCKY' CHANGED HIS LIFE
Fox News may be compensated for or earn a commission if you buy through our referral links.
"The Steps: A Memoir" by Sylvester Stallone is out now. (William Morrow)

"I think it comes from naïveté and the folly of youth, that you still have this sense of, 'I can do it, I can break the mold,'" Stallone said. "I hadn't been beaten enough by life yet to say it's over because, as an actor, if you haven't made it by 30, I'd say 99% you're never going to make it. I wasn't aware of that, so I kept going."
Sylvester Stallone has written a new memoir, "The Steps: A Memoir." (2026 NBCUniversal Media, LLC)

"In New York, when I was really down and out, I didn't focus on, 'God, you're going to be destitute,'" Stallone said. "There was this certain optimism that if you put every effort forward, if you denied yourself every moment of pleasure of going to the movies, dating a girl — if you abandoned all that and dedicate yourself, I believe that you'll know 100% whether you actually have a chance to be this character you always wished you could be."
Stallone never stopped believing he would one day make it as an actor.
WATCH: SYLVESTER STALLONE REFLECTS ON CHILDHOOD TRAUMA, ‘ROCKY’ AND WHY ‘TRYING’ MATTERS MOST

After leaving the American College in Switzerland without graduating and dropping out of the University of Miami just a few credits shy of a drama degree, Stallone returned to New York City with little to his name. He rented a room so cramped that he later compared it to the minimum size recommended for a federal jail cell. He shared a bathroom with 10 other people.

Stallone also found work as an usher at a movie theater, earning just $34 a week. He said the job became an education in filmmaking. Night after night, he studied the movies he watched, keeping his dream alive.
Sylvester Stallone is seen here in New York City. (Ron Galella Collection via Getty Images)

Stallone said he would shower with his clothes on to save money on laundry. If he were lucky enough to find a bar of soap that didn't have a "strange hair" stuck to it, he would use it to lather up "my shirt, pants, underwear, socks — and myself."
Sylvester Stallone is seen here on Jan. 12, 1979. (Getty Images)

"I could never afford to go to a laundromat," Stallone said. "My wife thinks this is so gross, 'Why would you take a shower with your clothes on?' I said, 'It made sense to me at the time, rather than going down to the laundromat. But this was a tenement home. It was so bad. But you do what you could to survive.'"
To stave off hunger, Stallone would eat spoonfuls of cottage cheese, then down three or four raw eggs. In the book, he recalled later treating himself to chicken breast and apple juice.
Sylvester Stallone speaks onstage during "Sylvester Stallone In Conversation with Tracy Smith: The Steps" at 92NY on Sept. 28, 2026, in New York City. (Getty Images)

"It's the only thing that made sense numerically, financially," he said. "Of course, it's all wrong. It's terrible. I'm surprised I didn't get salmonella, really. It's really quite remarkable. But these two things at a certain time of year, because in the summer, the cottage cheese would rot, and the eggs would spoil.
GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE

American actor Sylvester Stallone strikes at a punching bag in a boxing ring while his coach, Burgess Meredith (1908-1997), watches during training at a gymnasium in a still from the movie, "Rocky." (United Artists/Courtesy of Getty Images)

"But if you brought it from around October, it would sit on your windowsill until March. So that became my refrigerator. And at the time, I just thought it was so convenient. No dishes. You drink the egg, so you don't have to wash anything. You didn't need a fork. And the cottage cheese, it's a spoon, and you throw the cup away."
Sylvester Stallone is seen here in New York City. (Bettmann Archive)

Stallone wrote in the book, "I wouldn't recommend this diet to anyone. But if you're young and poor, it will suffice, which is why I used eating raw eggs in 'Rocky' to give some insight into Rocky's ways of approaching his life."
Stallone had a dollar or two a day for food. He needed a job, and fast.
American actor and screenwriter Sylvester Stallone on the set of "F.I.S.T.," directed by Norman Jewison. (Corbis via Getty Images)
One of Stallone's earliest gigs was cleaning the lion cages at Central Park Zoo. The smell was bad enough — but it wasn't what frightened him.

"I also feared for my life," he wrote. "The lions were always close by, always watching. They looked through me. They were behind a set of bars, but that didn't stop the great sad creatures from wedging their huge snouts between the bars to sniff me out. The way they inhaled and exhaled made an eerie moaning sound, like they already knew what I was going to taste like."
Sylvester Stallone was so broke when he married his first wife, Sasha Czack, in 1974, that he wore a movie costume. (Bettmann Archive)

During that period, Stallone faced repeated rejection from agents, including one who criticized his deep voice and asymmetrical mouth — two traits that would later become signatures of his screen persona.
LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS
Sylvester Stallone takes still photos on location while shooting a film in Dubuque. (Bettmann Archive)

Walking home one day, he spotted a "Help Wanted" sign at Dover Delicatessen and took the 6 p.m.-to-2 a.m. shift. While he was able to save enough money for a coat to brave the city's bitter winter, it's one gig he doesn't miss.

"Every customer gets cranky over this and that, 'Hey, there's not enough coleslaw here. This sandwich should weigh an ounce and a half more,'" Stallone said with a laugh. "You'd be shocked. I learned to be a really good fish cutter, like for lox on bagels. I still would hear, 'I can't see through the salmon.' They wanted the cut so thin that you could actually see light. Oh man. And you're cutting your fingers off, too."
After years of traveling in Europe, Sylvester Stallone returned to his birthplace, New York City, in 1969. (Bettmann Archive)

"And then the characters that come in at two in the morning, the outrageous drunks and gangsters, unbelievable," Stallone continued. "You'd be shocked who walks into a place at two in the morning and wants a sandwich. So that's colorful. And of course, I ended up in jail, but that's only because of the stupid deli."
American actor Sylvester Stallone sits on a staircase holding the leash of a dog wearing a football jersey in a still from the movie "Rocky." (Getty Images)
"I thought I was living OK, a decent life," he said. "But by today's standards, you were on the cusp of oblivion."

After an altercation at the deli, Stallone found himself handcuffed in the back of a police car, still wearing his apron and name tag. He was sent to "The Tombs," New York's notoriously violent detention facility — or, as Stallone put it, "the place of nightmares." He was put into a 20-foot-by-20-foot holding cell with at least 25 other men. One man was already pounding another's head into a small hole that prisoners used as a toilet.
Sylvester Stallone wrote "Rocky" and starred as boxer Rocky Balboa. (Getty Images)
A criminal court judge eventually released Stallone.
PUT YOUR ENTERTAINMENT KNOWLEDGE TO THE TEST AND SEE HOW YOU SCORE
American actor Sylvester Stallone appears with actor, director and screenwriter Woody Allen on the set of "Bananas." (Corbis via Getty Images)
"I took the apron, balled it up and tossed it in the trash on the way out the door," he wrote.
Today, Stallone has zero regrets.

"If you don't sacrifice completely and fail, you'll suffer for the rest of your life going, 'Why didn't I try harder? Why didn't I use whatever God-given talent I had to be the absolute best?'" Stallone said. "If you fail, you can say, 'I tried.' People can never point a finger in your face and say, 'You didn't try hard enough.' But my biggest fear was that I would leave something on the table."

Sylvester Stallone appears in a scene from "The Lords of Flatbush" (1974) after his girlfriend tells him she is pregnant, and he takes her to a jeweler to buy a ring. (FilmPublicityArchive/United Archives via Getty Images)
Looking back, Stallone said those difficult years taught him a lesson that still resonates in "Rocky" decades later.

Actor Sylvester Stallone as Rocky Balboa, circa 1982. (James Drake/Getty Images)
"'Rocky' still points out that if you're willing to completely sacrifice good times, pleasure and escapism for the goal, it's really possible," he said. "There is no halfway point."

title: Halle Berry's attorney fires back after ex Olivier Martinez accuses actress of abusing their son

story: Halle Berry’s attorney says Olivier Martinez’s claims she abused their son are "meritless." Martinez was granted a temporary restraining order from the actress, according to TMZ. (This video contains AI-assisted content.)
Halle Berry’s attorney fired back Thursday, calling claims made by her ex that she abused their son "meritless."
Olivier Martinez was granted a temporary restraining order from the actress Thursday, according to TMZ.
Martinez is also seeking sole custody of their 12-year-old son, alleging that she physically and emotionally abused the boy, according to documents obtained by People magazine and TMZ.

Martinez claims Berry caused him "emotional and mental distress due to physical abuse of our minor child, Maceo," adding that she "physically abused our son, Maceo, by jumping on him, putting her hands around his neck, and choking him," according to People.

Olivier Martinez was granted a temporary restraining order from Halle Berry. (WireImage)

The former couple have also been ordered to attend confidential mediation about custody.

Martinez claims Maceo called him after the incident and claimed she had attacked him. He also said Berry’s fiancé, Van Hunt, was at home at the time.
The petition also calls for Berry to not be under the influence and to undergo sobriety testing before, during and after any visits with their son.
Representatives for Martinez did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment.
The former couple finalized their divorce in 2023, eight years after they split.

In the settlement, the actress agreed to pay nearly $8,000 in monthly child support for their son, according to court documents obtained by Fox News Digital. She also pays Martinez 4.3% on any income she makes that exceeds $2 million.

title: Wynonna Judd says she and sister Ashley aren't speaking as family pain resurfaces
summary: Wynonna Judd reveals she and sister Ashley Judd aren't speaking right now as she prepares to release her deeply personal new country music album.
story: Wynonna Judd told Fox News Digital, her and her mom Naomi Judd's shared love of music helped them "bypass the bullcrap" and build a close relationship.
Wynonna Judd is finally telling her story – even the parts that may be painful for her family to hear.
The country star revealed she and sister Ashley Judd aren’t speaking right now, explaining that the two are not "connected" at the moment and focusing on their separate lives.

The revelation comes as Wynonna prepares to release her deeply personal new album Oct. 2, a project that prompted her to confront the complicated relationship she shared with her late mother, Naomi Judd, long-held family secrets and the anger and forgiveness she has wrestled with over the years.

"I feel like this is the most honest and vulnerable I’ve ever been," she told the outlet about writing "The Hard Truth." "It’s there for everyone to hear. So there are some days I think, ‘Oh my God, what have I done?’ And then other days I think, ‘There comes a point in your life when you are ready to tell your testimony.’"

Wynonna gained fame as one-half of the mother-daughter duo The Judds, whose close harmonies and roots-driven sound helped define country music in the 1980s. Between 1984 and 1991, they scored 20 Top 10 country hits, including 14 No. 1 singles, and won five Grammy Awards, nine CMA Awards and seven ACM Awards.

title: 'Yellowstone' star Neal McDonough refuses to watch hit series for ‘painful’ reason
summary: Neal McDonough played Malcolm Beck on "Yellowstone" but has never seen the show, calling his method acting memories "traumatic and painful."
story: The actor explained that his wife gave him an ultimatum when it came to his drinking, which ultimately got him to stop.
Neal McDonough may be known as one of the most ruthless villains in the "Yellowstone" universe, but there's one thing the actor himself has never done: watched the show.
McDonough, 60, portrayed ruthless businessman Malcolm Beck on the hit Taylor Sheridan series, appearing in six episodes during Season 2.
But reliving the performance is something McDonough admitted he avoids.
JEFF BRIDGES NEARLY PLAYED JOHN DUTTON BEFORE KEVIN COSTNER LANDED 'YELLOWSTONE' ROLE
Neal McDonough said he has never watched his performance on "Yellowstone." (Jesse Grant/Getty Images for A+E Networks )
"I've never seen it. You know, I don't watch any of my stuff," McDonough said on the "Arroyo Grande" podcast.
He went on to explain why he refuses to watch himself on screen.

"As a method actor, I can tell you if I look at a frame – that's why I don't watch any of my stuff. If I look at a frame of a show from 20 years ago, I know exactly the thought I was thinking. I know the song I was thinking about. I know where I was going. So going back to me sometimes can be really kind of traumatic and painful," he shared.
Even attending his own movie premieres doesn't necessarily mean he'll watch the finished product.

And McDonough isn't losing sleep over whether he delivered in a particular scene.

"I was there on the day," he said. "I know I did a great job because God gave me a talent. I'm terrible at pounding nails. I'm not very good at telling jokes. title: ‘Double Lives of Suburban Wives’ star's staggering $550K month after leaving teaching for adult content
summary: Brianna Coppage reveals her best month earned $550,000 in adult content, dwarfing her former teacher salary after losing her school position.
story: Former high school English teacher Brianna Coppage tells Fox News Digital she earns more in one month than she made in a year teaching and explains why she would "never" return to the classroom.
Brianna Coppage may have lost her teaching career, but she certainly didn't take a pay cut.

The "Double Lives of Suburban Wives" star told Fox News Digital that her adult-content business has transformed her family's finances, revealing that her most successful month brought in a staggering $550,000.
"Oh, my best month was 550,000," Brianna told Fox News Digital.
‘DOUBLE LIVES’ STAR REVEALS STAGGERING $550K MONTH AFTER LEAVING TEACHING CAREER

The figure marks a dramatic departure from her former life as an English teacher at St. Clair High School in Franklin County, Missouri. In 2023, Coppage was placed on administrative leave after her adult-content work was discovered. She later resigned from her position.
Asked whether she now makes more in a single month than she previously earned in an entire year as a teacher, Brianna didn't hesitate.
"Yes," she said.
'DOUBLE LIVES' STAR SAYS BEING KICKED OUT OF CHURCH OVER ADULT CONTENT CAREER DIDN'T SHAKE HER FAITH
And despite the controversy that followed the end of her teaching career, Brianna said she wouldn't go back even if given the opportunity.
"Never. Never," she told Fox News Digital when asked whether she would accept her teaching job back tomorrow.
"Yeah, just the lifestyle and the time and being able to just be in control of myself and in my business," she continued. "It's changed my family's life and just everything for the better."

Brianna is one of the women featured on TLC's "Double Lives of Suburban Wives," which follows six couples in the St. Louis area navigating marriage, parenthood and suburban life while maintaining careers creating adult content.

According to TLC, what began as a financial pivot for Brianna and her husband, Phillip, quickly became a lucrative business. But that success came with consequences when Brianna's online career was publicly exposed and she lost her teaching job.

Brianna told Fox News Digital that she still struggles with whether losing her career was justified.

"I think… it's a difficult concept to even wrap my mind around," she said. "So obviously like professions have a level of professionalism, but also they couldn't cite anything that I technically broke."
"So was I really doing anything wrong? I don't know," she continued. "I think it's on a basis of morality."
Brianna also pushed back on what she described as a misconception surrounding her former employment.
"There was no like morality clause, which is a lot of… there's a misconception about that, that I signed something or a clause, a morality clause," she said. "There wasn't one. So I don't know."
While losing her teaching career forced Brianna onto a different professional path, she said the financial impact of her new work has been life-changing.
Brianna Coppage said working alongside husband Phillip has brought financial success while also testing boundaries within their marriage. (TLC)
"My family was able to pay off all of our debts. I paid off my student loans," she told Fox News Digital. "So I stopped putting groceries on credit cards."
"Like yeah, it just is so freeing, and I don't know, it's been life-changing."

That financial freedom is one of the central tensions explored on "Double Lives of Suburban Wives," where the women weigh the benefits of their unconventional careers against the judgment and loss of privacy that can accompany them.
For Brianna, the cost has been significant.

"I think the greatest thing it has cost me is the privacy, the lack of privacy," she told Fox News Digital.
Being thrust into the public eye has sometimes left her feeling as though people forget there's a person behind the headlines.
"And being in the public eye, it's like, I'm not a human anymore," Brianna said. "I'm not normal just like everybody else when truly I am. Like we are human beings too."
But when weighing that loss against what her new career has made possible for her family, Brianna said the benefits extend far beyond her income.
"I think the greatest thing it has afforded is just memories and time with my family that I wouldn't trade for the world," she said.
‘DOUBLE LIVES’ STAR OPENS UP ABOUT MARRIAGE ‘BETRAYAL’ AFTER ADULT-CONTENT CAREER CHANGES HER LIFE
Brianna said her own upbringing has shaped how she views the opportunities she can now provide for her children.
"Like growing up, I grew up fairly poor. And I mean family vacations and letting my kids experience things that I never would have is really priceless."

Asked how she would respond if her daughter came to her as an adult and said she wanted to pursue the same kind of work, Brianna said her first priority would be making sure she understood what she was getting into.
DREA DE MATTEO SAYS ONLYFANS BECAME ‘POLITICAL STATEMENT’ AFTER FINANCIAL STRUGGLES THREATENED HER HOME
Promotional artwork for TLC's "Double Lives of Suburban Wives." (TLC)

Her success hasn't eliminated the complications that come with mixing marriage and business.

She added that she was glad viewers were seeing some of those difficulties rather than an artificially polished version of their marriage.
