title: Piers Morgan questions Princess Diana’s brother’s explosive claims about King Charles after error about him
summary: Piers Morgan argues that Charles Spencer's memoir mistake undermines explosive claims about King Charles III's reaction to Princess Diana's death.
story: Piers Morgan argues an inaccurate account about him raises questions about Charles Spencer's recollections of conversations following Princess Dianas death.
Piers Morgan says Charles Spencer's public apology isn't enough.

The British broadcaster told Fox News Digital he is still pursuing legal action over what he calls defamatory passages in Spencer's memoir, "Swan Song: Diana, My Sister," even after Spencer acknowledged a factual error and apologized.

"He's published an egregious defamatory lie about me, and that lie remains in copies of the book being sold all over the world, including the United States," Morgan told Fox News Digital. "Although he's rushed out an apology and admitted that it was completely untrue what he said about me, he hasn't removed it from the book."
KING CHARLES, PRINCE WILLIAM 'FURIOUS' AS PRINCESS DIANA'S BROTHER UNLEASHES EXPLOSIVE CLAIMS: EXPERTS

Piers Morgan, left, told Fox News Digital he is still pursuing legal action against Charles Spencer, right, Princess Diana's brother, following the publication of "Swan Song." (Yui Mok/PA Images via Getty Images; Max Mumby/Indigo/Getty Images)

"My legal team has been in touch with him and his publishers demanding that they remove the book from sale and reissue the book without the offending pages," Morgan said. "It's not just a one-off reference. We're talking about several pages here."
Spencer denied that Morgan had sued him, prompting Morgan to release correspondence from his lawyers showing they had contacted Spencer and his publisher, The Sun reported.

Copies of Charles Spencer's book about his sister, Diana, Princess of Wales, are displayed on its publication day at Foyles on Charing Cross Road in London, England, on Sept. 22, 2026. The book, "Swan Song: Diana, My Sister," recounts Earl Spencer's childhood with Diana. King Charles is quoted in the book as saying, "We'll forget her soon enough." (In Pictures via Getty Images)
Morgan wants any damages paid to The King's Trust, a youth charity King Charles III founded in 1976 as the Prince of Wales.
WATCH: PIERS MORGAN CHALLENGES CHARLES SPENCER'S CLAIMS ABOUT KING CHARLES
Fox News Digital reached out to Penguin Press, the U.S. publisher of "Swan Song," and Althorp for comment.

The book incorrectly identifies Morgan as the editor of the Daily Mirror when Mirror Group newspapers published photographs of Diana exercising in a gym in November 1993, People magazine reported. According to the outlet, Morgan was working at The Sun at the time and didn't become editor of the Daily Mirror until 1995.
Princess Diana leaves a press conference at the Hilton Hotel in London on Dec. 3, 1993. (Getty Images)
Spencer acknowledged the error but stood by his recollection that Morgan was "surly and annoyed" when Spencer called Morgan to tell him he was not welcome at Diana's 1997 funeral.
Charles Spencer, Princess Diana's brother, attends a reception celebrating the "Diana: A Celebration" exhibit at the National Constitution Center in Philadelphia on Oct. 1, 2009. (Getty Images)

"Earl Spencer's account of his conversation with Piers Morgan is accurate," read a statement published by People magazine. "Mr. Morgan was surly and annoyed when Earl Spencer called personally to tell him that he was not welcome at his sister's funeral."
Daily Mirror editor Piers Morgan sits in his office at Canary Wharf, London, on Dec. 14, 1998. (Getty Images)

"The book then records Earl Spencer's assumption that Mr. Morgan's response was because he was editor of the Daily Mirror when the Mirror Group had published highly intrusive photographs of Princess Diana at the gym," the statement continued.

Charles Spencer has apologized to Piers Morgan for a factual error in his new memoir, "Swan Song: Diana, My Sister." However, he stands by his account of their phone conversation in 1997. (Jordan Pettitt/PA Images)
"As a historian, accuracy is important to Earl Spencer. He therefore wishes to clarify that his assumption was incorrect. Earl Spencer apologizes to Mr. Morgan for this error."
GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE
"Swan Song: Diana, My Sister," written by Charles Spencer, is displayed at a bookstore in London, United Kingdom, on Sept. 22, 2026. (Anadolu via Getty Images)

People reported that the passage will be corrected in the second edition of "Swan Song." Spencer has not withdrawn his account of the conversation itself, only his mistaken assumption that Morgan was editor of the Daily Mirror at the time.
Morgan said the error casts doubt on the accuracy of other claims in the memoir, including Spencer's account of what King Charles allegedly said after Diana's death.

Britain's Prince Charles kisses Lady Sarah McCorquodale while her sister Lady Jane Fellows looks on at RAF Northolt Airport near London on Aug. 31, 1997, after the arrival of Charles and the casket containing the body of his former wife, Diana, Princess of Wales. Diana died in a car crash in Paris earlier that morning. (AFP via Getty Images)

"He's claiming to be a historian," Morgan said. "He says he's written this as a work of historical record to set the record straight about his sister, Princess Diana, one of the most talked-about people, obviously, of modern times. But he makes incredibly incendiary allegations against our now-king, Prince Charles, in which he claims that within hours of Diana dying, he spoke to Prince Charles on the phone and Prince Charles sounded as giddy as a lottery winner with excitement that Diana had died."

Prince William and Prince Harry stand with Prince Charles holding a funeral program at Westminster Abbey for the funeral of Diana, Princess of Wales, in London. (Tim Graham Photo Library via Getty Images)

"It's hard to imagine a more disgusting thing to say," Morgan said. "I don't believe for a moment that Charles was like that. In fact, I had Paul Burrell, Diana's former butler, on my show last week saying that he saw the prince in Paris within hours of Diana dying and the man was a broken man. [He] was utterly grief-stricken. So why this matters about what happened to me is that people have been questioning the accuracy of his memory of these phone calls with King Charles."

Paul Burrell, butler to Diana, Princess of Wales, stands in the background as she makes a three-day visit to Bosnia-Herzegovina to raise awareness about land mines and call for a complete ban on their production, sale and use. The trip was organized by the American-based Landmine Survivors Network. The photo was taken Aug. 10, 1997. (Getty Images)

In the book, Spencer recalled a conversation with then-Prince Charles about whether Diana's sons, Prince William and Prince Harry, then 15 and 12, would walk behind her coffin during the funeral procession. Spencer said a royal aide informed him about the plan and that he opposed it. Charles then called Spencer, leading to what Spencer described as a heated exchange.
Prince Harry, Prince Charles, Earl Spencer and Prince William stand at Westminster Abbey during the funeral service for Diana, Princess of Wales, on Sept. 6, 1997. (Getty Images)

"Prince Charles continued his stream of anger, without me interrupting," Spencer wrote. "Then he stopped. I assumed the pause signaled an effort to bring himself under control, but then he unleashed down the phone what I have always taken to be his pent-up contempt for Diana, and his horror that the world was so bowled over by her death. 'Rest assured,' he hissed, 'we'll forget her soon enough!'"
LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

Diana, Princess of Wales, wearing a green suit with a velvet collar designed by Amanda Wakeley, gives a speech announcing her resignation from public duties during a Headway charity lunch at the Hilton Hotel in London on Dec. 3, 1993. (Getty Images)
Spencer wrote that he was "so stunned" that he took a few seconds before replying, "I can't believe you just said that," and hanging up.

A Buckingham Palace spokesperson said in a statement, "While we do not comment on books as a matter of principle, His Majesty is mindful that the pain of fraternal grief can cloud reason, affect judgment and color memory in ways others do not recognize, even many years after such a loss."
Prince William and Prince Harry look at floral tributes to Diana, Princess of Wales, outside Kensington Palace in London, England, on Sept. 5, 1997. (WireImage)
A palace spokesperson told Fox News Digital they had no further comment.

"It is not every day you wake up to find you’ve been gaslit by the king," Spencer told the BBC. "It was astonishingly provocative and below the belt because it was essentially trying to say I’d lied without the king being able to deny what I’d said." (Getty Images)
Spencer has stood by the account, telling the BBC, "I'm telling the truth."
Morgan rejected Spencer's account.
Prince Charles and Diana's sisters Lady Sarah McCorquodale and Jane Fellowes are seen here on Aug. 31, 1997, following Princess Diana's death in a car crash. (AFP via Getty Images)

"I can't imagine for a moment [the king] would say that about the mother of his children," Morgan said. "This goes to the heart of the credibility of the book. If he can get something so grotesquely wrong about me over several pages, which is so easy to check and prove he got it wrong, then why should we believe him about anything he says about King Charles? That's why it matters."
PUT YOUR ENTERTAINMENT KNOWLEDGE TO THE TEST AND SEE HOW YOU SCORE

"Earl Spencer has apologized to me for his defamatory lies published in his new book, 'Swan Song,' published today," Morgan wrote on X on Sept. 22, 2026. "But I am pursuing legal action against him and his publisher Penguin to have the lies removed, and damages paid to the King’s Trust." (REUTERS/Henry Nicholls)
Morgan also disputes Spencer's recollection of their phone call.

"His account of how he did that and how I was with him is completely untrue," Morgan said. "He says that I was snarling, I was rude, I was all these things. I would simply ask people, how realistic is that? This guy's just lost his sister. Is it likely that I, as a newspaper editor who was very friendly with Diana, friendly with her mother and Earl Spencer's mother, that I would treat a family member in a snarling or rude manner? I don’t think it is."
Diana, Princess of Wales, and her mother, Frances Shand Kydd, are seen here on Sept. 16, 1989. (Getty Images)

"At the end of the call, I said to him that I would like him to pass on my deepest condolences to his mother, who I knew very well. And he said he would do that and thanked me. That's not a snarly, rude conversation."
Diana, Princess of Wales, died in 1997. She was 36. (Tim Graham Photo Library via Getty Images)
Morgan said he wrote about the phone call in his 2005 book, "The Insider."
"I put it to people that if he's so wrong about the tone of my conversation with him that week, then why should we believe him when he says that Charles was giddy with excitement?"

Royal experts told Fox News Digital that Prince William and King Charles are reportedly furious following the recent publication of Earl Charles Spencer's memoir about his late sister, Princess Diana. (Aaron Chown - WPA Pool/Getty Images)
Spencer told People magazine during an interview at Althorp that his duty as a historian is "to lay down facts."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Visitors are seen here at Althorp House, Princess Diana's ancestral home. (David Levenson/Getty Images)
"And that's what I'm doing," he told the outlet. "There's no viciousness. I'm not resentful or bitter or any of those things."
Spencer said his priority was to honor his sister.
"The central person, the only one that really matters, is Diana," he said.
Stephanie Nolasco is an Entertainment Reporter for Fox News Digital.

title: Pete Davidson calls out NYC Mayor Zohran Mamdani over highway mess
summary: Pete Davidson called out NYC Mayor Zohran Mamdani on "Jimmy Kimmel Live!" over the BQE's endless construction to thunderous studio applause.
story: The organization PETA Kills Animals bought a billboard in New York Citys Times Square backing Pete Davidsons puppy purchase.  (Julia Bonavita/Fox News Digital)
Pete Davidson didn’t hold back while delivering a blunt message to New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani.

On Monday night, the 32-year-old comedian appeared on "Jimmy Kimmel Live!" where Kimmel, 58, told him that Mamdani, 34, would be his next guest. The late night host then pointed out that Davidson was a "lifelong resident of this city" and asked if he had any questions for the mayor.
"Yes, could he fix the "f---ing BQE, please?" Davidson said in a clip shared on the show's Instagram page.
Pete Davidson called out New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani over the long-delayed construction on a major highway. (Todd Owyoung/NBC via Getty Images; Michael M. Santiago/Getty Images)
NYC DRIVERS SHELL OUT $9 CONGESTION TOLL. CITY ADMITS IT FAILED TO IMPROVE AIR QUALITY
The BQE, short for the Brooklyn-Queens Expressway, is a major New York City highway that runs through Brooklyn and Queens and has long been criticized for traffic congestion and aging infrastructure.
Davidson's request was immediately met with cheers and thunderous applause from the studio audience.
"You hit on something," Kimmel noted.
"Look at that," Davidson said, gesturing toward the crowd.
"That's the loudest response I've ever gotten," he added with a laugh.
Davidson told Kimmel to ask Mamdani about the highway that he says has "been under construction since before I was born." (Disney via Getty Images)
The "Saturday Night Live" star went on to explain that his frustration stemmed from the seemingly endless construction and what he described as a lack of visible work at the site.
MAMDANI'S LATEST FREEBIE SETS OFF ONLINE FURY AS CRITICS RIP CITY PRIORITIES: 'OPERA SOCIALISM'

"The BQE has been under construction since before I was born. And here’s my problem with it," Davidson said. "They’re never doing anything. Someone’s just standing there eating a sandwich or on the phone, and there’s all these cones around."
"So I don't know what mob front or whatever, who's getting money from whatever, but just fix it, please," he added.
ZOHRAN MAMDANI ADMITS HE WANTS TO END HIS ‘ONE-SIDED BEEF’ ABOUT TAXES WITH RAPPER 50 CENT
"I'm going to ask him about it. I will ask him about it," Kimmel assured Davidson, who replied, "Yeah, please!"
At the end of Mamdani's appearance on the show, Kimmel presented the mayor with Davidson's question.
"One more thing," Kimmel told Mamdani.
"Hit me," Mamdani said with a smile.
Mamdani later responded to Davidson's message when he appeared on Kimmel's show later in the episode. (ABC/JimmyKimmelLive)
"Pete Davidson wants to know what's going on in the BQE," Kimmel said. "He says he drives by it and he sees nobody doing anything. He said it's been like since before he was born."

Mamdani responded by highlighting his office’s BQE Central Project, a $4 billion plan to rehabilitate the city-owned section of the Brooklyn-Queens Expressway between Atlantic Avenue and Sands Street, with construction expected to begin in 2030.

"We're gonna be putting a multibillion-dollar plan to actually repair the part the city owns," Mamdani said. "Which is the part that is currently the most at risk and that's going to be proceeding over the next 10 years. Full safety. No diversion of traffic into local neighborhoods and actually bring it back."
"So you’re saying Pete’s daughter will also be complaining about this," Kimmel joked as Mamdani and the audience laughed.
Fox News Digital reached out to Davidson's and Mamdani's reps for comment.

Mamdani, a Democratic socialist, emerged as a surprise winner in New York City’s mayoral race last November after building a strong following through social media and grassroots campaigning. He took office on Jan. 1 when he was sworn in as mayor.
Mamdani, a Democratic socialist, pulled off a surprise election victory last November. (Barry Williams/New York Daily News/Tribune News Service via Getty Images)
Davidson has mostly talked about politics jokingly, but he has openly criticized President Donald Trump and supported the Democratic presidential nominee Hillary Clinton during the 2016 election.
After Clinton lost the 2016 election, Davidson posted an angry pro-Clinton message and later got a tattoo of the former secretary of state, calling her his "hero."
In an interview with Variety that was published Wednesday, Davidson discussed how he is in the process of removing nearly all of his almost 200 tattoos.

"One, they were f---in' horrible," he said of his tattoos. "Two, it was a business decision. I hated coming into the makeup trailer three hours early to spray-paint over horrible f---in' tattoos. And third, I was like, ‘I’m not this dude.’ I got these when I was in an immense amount of pain, and I was trying to show people my pain."
Davidson admitted that some of his tattoos were a result of his past struggles with self-harm, saying he initially used the ink to cover scars.
"I used to cut, so some of [the tattoos] covered up the cuts," he told Variety.

Davidson is removing most of his 200 tattoos but vowed to keep his Hillary Clinton ink. (Dominik Bindl/Getty Images)
However, Davidson confirmed that he would be keeping his Clinton tattoo despite removing most of his other ink.

title: Silent heart threat found in adults under 30 with no known cardiovascular disease
summary: Silent artery plaque was detected in over half of healthy adults in the REACT study, yet traditional cardiovascular risk scores missed many of those cases.
story: Dr. Jason A. Gluck, vice chair of the Heart & Vascular Institute and system chief of cardiology at AtlantiCare in New Jersey, discusses a recent study that found stroke incidence has more than doubled among young adults.
A buildup of artery-clogging plaque may begin much earlier than many people realize, new research has found.

About one in 13 adults ages 18 to 29 already had silent atherosclerosis, the hardening of the arteries from plaque, despite having no known cardiovascular disease, while more than half of all healthy adults in the study showed signs of plaque somewhere in their arteries, according to a major new international study.
Researchers from Denmark and Spain used advanced imaging to examine more than 16,800 adults ages 18 to 70 with no known cardiovascular disease.

They found plaque in 57.1% of participants, with prevalence increasing steadily with age, from about one in 13 adults under 30 to roughly nine in 10 adults ages 60 to 70, according to the research published in The New England Journal of Medicine in August.
EVERYDAY HABIT LINKED TO DRAMATICALLY LOWER RISK OF DYING FROM HEART DISEASE

Atherosclerosis occurs when fatty deposits, cholesterol and other substances build up inside arteries, according to experts. The process often develops silently over many years before causing a heart attack or stroke.
A new study found signs of silent artery plaque in some healthy young adults with no known cardiovascular disease. (iStock)

"For decades, we have estimated cardiovascular risk using factors such as age, blood pressure and cholesterol," Dr. Borja Ibáñez, a cardiologist and scientific director of Spain's National Center for Cardiovascular Research (CNIC), said in a statement.
"This study shows that we can now go one step further and detect the disease directly before it causes a heart attack or stroke."
COMMON CHOLESTEROL DRUG LINKED TO LOWER DEMENTIA RISK WHEN STARTED EARLY

The new findings come from the first phase of the ongoing international REACT study, which is mapping how common silent artery plaque is across adulthood. In the next phase, researchers will test whether earlier detection can improve heart disease prevention.
Researchers are studying whether earlier detection of artery plaque could improve heart disease prevention. (iStock)

"Until now, preventive decisions have been based on an estimate of risk, but we did not know whether the disease was already present," Henning Bundgaard, professor of cardiology at Rigshospitalet in Copenhagen, said.
"REACT shows that atherosclerosis can be detected decades before clinical manifestations appear and provides the most comprehensive atlas of the evolution of the disease across adult life."
MAN GOES TO DOCTOR TO PROVE HE’S ‘IN PERFECT SHAPE’; TEST REVEALS SHOCKING DIAGNOSIS
The study also revealed that men tended to develop plaque five to 10 years earlier than women, while women experienced their steepest increase between ages 40 and 60.
Knowing your blood pressure, cholesterol and other heart health risk factors can help reduce the risk of cardiovascular disease, experts say. (iStock)

Researchers also found that commonly used cardiovascular risk scores only identified a small proportion of people who already had silent atherosclerosis, suggesting some cases may go undetected using traditional risk assessments alone.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS
While the researchers believe portable ultrasound could eventually help identify hidden plaque earlier, they said further clinical trials are needed.
The findings should encourage people to take heart health seriously but not to panic, experts note.
Researchers say heart disease prevention should begin early, even before symptoms appear. (iStock)
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER

"Finding plaque doesn't mean someone is about to have a heart attack, but finding it gives us an opportunity to address a patient's risk factors," Dr. Sirisha Vadali, a cardiologist at HonorHealth Women’s Heart Health in Arizona who was not involved in the research, told Fox News Digital.
"We shouldn't wait for symptoms to start paying attention to heart health. Feeling healthy doesn't necessarily mean your arteries are free of plaque."
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
She cautioned that the study alone does not establish that screening everyone will directly prevent heart attacks or strokes.
Healthy lifestyle habits, including avoiding tobacco, staying active and eating a nutritious diet, can help protect heart health, experts say. (iStock)
Vadali stressed that the findings do not mean everyone under 30 should undergo artery screening, saying decisions about additional testing should be based on a person's individual risk factors.

She recommended avoiding tobacco, staying physically active and eating a diet rich in vegetables, fruits, beans, whole grains, nuts and fish while limiting saturated fat and excess sodium to help protect heart health.

title: One group of married Americans is having more sex — and happier marriages
summary: The Institute for Family Studies research finds regular churchgoers report more frequent sex and greater sexual satisfaction than nonreligious spouses.
story: Jessica Steinman, a Los Angeles-based marriage therapist, discusses new findings that married couples who regularly attend church report having more frequent sex and greater sexual satisfaction than those who attend less often or not at all.

Married couples who regularly attend church report having more frequent sex and greater sexual satisfaction than those who attend less often or not at all, according to a new report from the Institute for Family Studies (IFS) in Charlottesville, Virginia.

Researchers analyzed findings from multiple datasets, including the 2026 IFS Religion and Family Survey of 3,125 married adults ages 18–54, the long-running nationally representative General Social Survey and a separate survey of 1,219 alumni of FOCUS, a Catholic campus ministry.

Regular churchgoers reported having more frequent sex than less religious or non-religious married adults, with regularly attending Catholics reporting some of the highest levels of sexual frequency. The association remained even after accounting for demographic differences.
COMMON MARRIAGE HABIT COULD QUIETLY KILL YOUR SEX LIFE, EXPERT WARNS
Among married adults ages 20 to 54, 62% of regular churchgoers reported having sex at least once a week, compared with 48% of nonreligious spouses, according to the report.

In addition to frequency, sexual satisfaction was also higher among church attendants. Catholics and Protestants who regularly attended religious services were more likely to rate their sex lives positively than those who attended less often or had no religious affiliation.
Married couples who regularly attend church report having more frequent sex and greater sexual satisfaction than those who attend less often or not at all, according to a new report. (iStock)
Daily prayer was linked to greater sexual satisfaction among married Catholics and Protestants, though it was not associated with more frequent sex.

Among churchgoers, 55% of Catholics and 45% of Protestants rated their sex lives as "excellent" or "very good," compared with 45% of nominal Catholics, 35% of nominal Protestants and 40% of religiously unaffiliated respondents.
‘QUIET QUITTING’ IN MARRIAGE: THE SUBTLE SIGNS A SPOUSE HAS EMOTIONALLY CHECKED OUT

Those who viewed marriage as a permanent commitment were more likely to report both frequent and satisfying sex. That belief, along with shared values, was also strongly associated with overall marital quality.
Study limitations
Because the analysis was observational, it cannot determine whether religious practice directly causes better marital or sexual outcomes, the authors acknowledged.
Additionally, the marital outcomes were self-reported, and other unmeasured differences between religious and non-religious respondents could have influenced the results.

Regular churchgoers reported having more frequent sex than less religious or non-religious married adults, with regularly attending Catholics reporting some of the highest levels of sexual frequency. (iStock)
Differences in factors such as age and length of marriage could also make it challenging to strike comparisons with the broader population.
The study was funded by FOCUS, the Fellowship of Catholic University Students.
Marriage therapist reacts

Jessica Steinman, a licensed marriage and family therapist and certified sex addiction therapist in Los Angeles, spoke with Fox News Digital about the potential relationship between religious activity and the quality of a couple’s sex life.

"When we think of people who are really involved in religion … we might think they're not having a lot of sex or that they're having very constricted views on their sex lives," she said. "And this article and research show that's changing."
WHY COUPLES SHOULD FLIRT WITH EACH OTHER EVERY DAY — PLUS THE ‘RED FLAG’ TO AVOID

People who actively participate in a shared spiritual or religious life may also feel more connected to one another as partners, according to Steinman, who is also the chief clinical officer for No Matter What Recovery in Los Angeles, Chicago and Austin.
The rituals and shared practices associated with religious life likely play a role in strengthening that connection, the expert suggested. (iStock)

"If they're showing up and looking at things outside themselves — things that are spiritual, things that are religious, things that are having them look inward, things that are having them look into larger morals and values within their marriages and partnerships — I think they're going to possibly have happier marriages and partnerships," the therapist said.

They may also be more vulnerable and open with one another, which could contribute to a more active sex life, she added.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
The rituals and shared practices associated with religious life likely play a role in strengthening that connection, the expert suggested.
Religious couples who attend church together may also be more vulnerable and open with one another, which could contribute to a more active sex life, an expert noted. (iStock)

"Certain religious settings are really focused on rituals and traditions," Steinman said. "And if you're looking at partnership and marriage … engaging in sexual connection and sexual intimacy can really become a ritual itself."
The research highlighted what has been described as an ongoing "sex recession" during which people are not engaging in sexual intimacy as much as they once did.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
Regardless of religious affiliation, Steinman encourages people to find ways to connect with their partners.
"Get off the phones, get off of the internet, turn the TV off and start really connecting with your partner," she advised.

Steinman suggested that partners engage with one another and build connections that go deeper than simply asking, "How was your day?"
That can include building emotional openness and discussing how partners want to connect sexually, she said.

title: Taking daily supplement may help preserve muscle as you age — even without exercise
summary: New research in the Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition links daily creatine to memory gains and sarcopenia prevention.
story: Jacob Zemer, a New York-based fitness coach who primarily trains clients ranging from 35 to 55 years old, said there are several reasons that adults start losing muscle as they get older.

Daily creatine supplementation could help middle-aged and older adults preserve lean muscle mass, gain strength and support cognitive function, whether it's paired with exercise or not, according to a study published in the Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition.
The 12-week study, conducted by researchers at Texas A&M University’s Exercise & Sport Nutrition Lab, evaluated 64 men and women ages 45 to 65.

Participants were divided into non-exercise and exercise-plus-diet groups, then randomly assigned to take either 10 grams of creatine monohydrate per day — administered in two 5-gram doses — or a placebo.
ONE MUSCLE PROTEIN MAY HOLD THE KEY TO STAYING STRONGER AS YOU AGE, STUDY FINDS

Creatine is a naturally occurring compound that helps cells regenerate adenosine triphosphate (ATP), the primary energy source for cellular activity in both muscle and brain tissue, according to Cleveland Clinic.
Creatine monohydrate is a dietary supplement that helps muscles produce quick energy during activities like strength training.

A 12-week study in the Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition found that taking 10 grams of creatine monohydrate daily helped middle-aged and older adults increase lean muscle mass and strength. (iStock)

Adults naturally lose muscle mass and strength as they age, a condition known as sarcopenia. While dieting can accelerate that muscle loss, the new study found that creatine monohydrate helped counter the effect.
FITNESS EXPERT REVEALS 6 THINGS PEOPLE OVER 35 SHOULD DO AFTER WORKOUTS TO STAY STRONG

Adding creatine to an exercise and diet intervention resulted in greater reductions in body fat percentage, better preservation of lean body mass, and marked improvements in upper- and lower-body strength compared to a placebo.

Even among participants who did not engage in exercise or dietary changes, daily creatine supplementation increased lean tissue mass and improved muscular strength and endurance, according to the study.
When combined with a resistance training and weight-loss program, creatine supplementation enhanced fat loss while preserving lean body mass. (iStock)

"The fact that you can increase lean muscle mass even without exercise is remarkable, especially as we age," New York-based fitness coach Jacob Zemer told Fox News Digital. "Between the physical and mental benefits, most people should be considering creatine supplementation."
The expert, who was not involved in the study, noted that even participants who did not exercise saw an increase in their bench press and leg press.
"The fact that you can increase lean muscle mass even without exercise is remarkable."
Zemer said the findings suggest creatine may help build actual muscle tissue that generates strength, rather than simply increasing the amount of water stored in muscle cells.
Beyond physical performance, the researchers found that the 10-gram daily dose of creatine supported improvements in select tests of memory and cognitive processing.
While creatine offers clear physical and cognitive benefits as adults age, experts emphasize that supplementation enhances — but does not replace — the primary benefits of regular exercise. (iStock)

"My main takeaway from the study is that the benefits of creatine extend far beyond just athletes and bodybuilders," Zemer said. "Creatine continues to be the most scientifically studied and validated supplement on the market."
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
However, the trainer emphasized that supplementation should not replace regular physical activity.
"Just because you can increase lean muscle mass by taking creatine without exercise does not mean that it is optimal or a replacement for exercise," Zemer cautioned.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
"The benefits of exercise will always supersede those of creatine alone, and when the two are combined, they are both enhanced."
Even without an exercise routine, participants who supplemented with creatine saw gains in lean tissue mass, upper- and lower-body strength, and markers of glycemic control. (iStock)
The study authors noted several limitations to their findings.

Participants chose whether to join the exercise or non-exercise groups before being randomly assigned to receive either creatine or a placebo, which could have introduced lifestyle differences between the groups.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Additionally, because the study lasted just 12 weeks and included only healthy adults, researchers don't yet know whether the benefits would be long-term or whether they would apply to people with serious metabolic or neurological conditions.

For those considering taking creatine, Zemer advised consulting a healthcare professional to determine whether it's right for them, then choosing a reputable brand, staying hydrated and taking it consistently.

The study authors noted several limitations, including participant self-selection into exercise groups, exploratory cognitive endpoints, and a 12-week timeframe that leaves long-term adaptations unexamined. (iStock)

"Recommended minimum dosages for creatine are typically 3 grams for women and 5 grams for men," he said. "This study used higher dosages. Creatine is about consistency rather than when you take it, so find a time you can consistently take it daily."
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
According to the NIH Office of Dietary Supplements, creatine is generally considered safe for healthy adults, although some people may experience bloating, stomach discomfort or water retention.
Experts recommend talking with a healthcare provider before beginning supplementation, particularly for those with kidney disease or other chronic health conditions.
Khloe Quill is a lifestyle writer with Fox News Digital. She and the lifestyle team cover a range of story topics including food and drink, travel, and health.

title: Men are hiding potentially deadly disorder amid pressure to build the 'perfect' body
summary: Sylvester Stallone's bulimia revelation spotlights a crisis experts say is surging among men and boys driven by looksmaxxing and musculature ideals.
story: Brian Pollack, a licensed clinical social worker and certified eating disorders specialist at Hilltop Behavioral Health in Summit, New Jersey, specializes in treating males who struggle with eating disorders, which he said is "highly underreported."
Days after Sylvester Stallone revealed his own history with bulimia, experts are highlighting a growing but often overlooked rise in eating disorders among men.
The Academy Award-nominated actor, 80, revealed during an interview with The New York Times that he developed an "obsession" with eating habits while prepping for his role in the 1982 movie "Rambo."

Stallone said he took pains to appear more "animalistic," drawing inspiration from jaguars and cats. "It became an obsession. Really bad. It got to the point where I became bulimic," he said during the interview.
SYLVESTER STALLONE REVEALS SURPRISING HEALTH STRUGGLE BEHIND HIS FAMOUSLY RIPPED PHYSIQUE

Bulimia nervosa is an eating disorder marked by episodes of binge-eating — consuming a large amount of food while feeling a loss of control — followed by purging behaviors such as vomiting, excessive use of laxatives or diuretics, fasting or excessive exercise, according to the National Institute of Mental Health (NIMH).
Experts are highlighting a growing but often overlooked rise in eating disorders among men. (iStock)

Brian Pollack, a licensed clinical social worker and certified eating disorders specialist at Hilltop Behavioral Health in Summit, New Jersey, specializes in treating males who struggle with eating disorders, which he said is "highly underreported."

According to the National Association of Anorexia Nervosa and Associated Disorders (ANAD), about 30 million Americans experience an eating disorder during their lifetime, and roughly one-third are male.
What's driving the trend?

"Guys with eating disorders just present differently — for some men, it's about musculature … they continue to build muscle because they are afraid that they are weak, they want their muscles to align," Pollack told Fox News Digital. "We also see people who want to be so lean and pencil-thin that they don't eat whatsoever."
The expert, who has not treated Stallone, compared today's body-image pressures on boys and men with the beauty ideals many girls and women faced during earlier decades.
MEN FACE NEW PRESSURE TO STAY ‘HOT’ AS THEY AGE — AND IT’S NOT JUST ABOUT LIVING LONGER

"We’re seeing this extreme need for perfection and musculature — and that is leading to bulimia right now," he told Fox News Digital. "It’s particularly in our adolescent boys, who are consuming a lot of information about the ideal of masculinity in the eyes of society at large."
Societal expectations of masculinity can make it harder for men to identify and express feelings of vulnerability or distress, according to Pollack.
With binging, there is a loss of control over food — and purging is a way to get back in control, the expert noted. (iStock)
"Bulimia, especially, is about control," he said. "And what is it that men want? They want to be in control on a superficial level."
With binging, there is a loss of control over food — and purging is a way to get back in control, Pollack noted.
COMMON GYM SUPPLEMENT COULD HELP FIGHT DEPRESSION, NEW RESEARCH SUGGESTS
The increase in bulimia and other eating disorders among men may also be driven by a desire to emulate celebrities.

"There's a big trend right now called ‘looksmaxxing,' where boys are harming themselves in pursuit of an ideal appearance, including undergoing cosmetic procedures to alter their jawlines," Pollack said. "It’s getting very scary out there, actually."
Warning signs

For many men, it may not be easy for others to recognize that they are struggling with bulimia or other eating disorders, as the binging and purging behaviors are usually done in secret, Pollack said.
"They're hidden," he said. "People are ashamed of them at times."

Some men become fixated on restrictive eating patterns, the expert said, including following strict ketogenic diets, consuming excessive amounts of protein, or eating only foods they consider "clean," such as organic, whole-food or non-GMO products. (iStock)
One red flag, he said, is if a loved one begins purchasing increasing amounts of supplements, such as creatine, or performance-enhancing substances such as human growth hormone.
People with eating disorders may exhibit compulsive behaviors around both exercise and eating, including working out for multiple hours every day and carefully calculating every aspect of their diet.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

Some men become fixated on restrictive eating patterns, Pollack said, including following strict ketogenic diets, consuming excessive amounts of protein or eating only foods they consider "clean," such as organic, whole-food or non-GMO products.
In some cases, the obsession becomes so extreme that men may avoid eating foods prepared elsewhere or outside their strict standards.
The expert said men often don't have the vocabulary to talk about emotional distress, making eating disorders harder to identify. (iStock)

Pollack said some people may have "cheat days" where they visit fast-food restaurants and eat as much as they can, in an attempt to satisfy an "intense urge" stoked by restriction. "They binge, and we often see people hiding in the bathroom within 45 minutes after meals."

Another warning sign is escalating use of laxatives or diuretics, with some people taking increasingly large amounts because smaller doses no longer produce the desired effect of feeling "emptied" or "in control."
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
Pollack emphasized that bulimia and other disorders are experienced among men at all ages, from middle school and high school through college and adulthood.
"This is real, and men are afraid to talk about it," he said. "There's a real issue."

Bulimia is known to have life-threatening health impacts. "Just on a baseline level, with someone who purges, we see electrolyte imbalances, along with kidney and liver damage," an eating disorders specialist said. (iStock)
The expert said men often don't have the vocabulary to talk about emotional distress, making eating disorders harder to identify.

Instead, Pollack recommended asking questions about body goals — such as whether someone is trying to "sculpt your body" or "make sure that you have a six-pack" — and whether those pursuits are helping them avoid confronting difficult emotions.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
Health effects
Bulimia is known to have life-threatening health impacts. "Just on a baseline level, with someone who purges, we see electrolyte imbalances, along with kidney and liver damage," Pollack said.
The expert shared that he has seen people go into cardiac arrest because prolonged malnutrition and repeated purging had severely damaged their hearts.
Bulimia patients may face expensive dental work, he added, due to severe erosion of their tooth enamel.
Esophagus issues, such as acid reflux and GERD, may also develop due to purging.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Long-term medical issues can range from treating heartburn with over-the-counter medication to facing life-threatening issues, Pollack said.
"It's a very serious scenario."

title: Kratom industry warns synthetic opioids should not be called 'kratom'
summary: The American Kratom Association claims products found near two dead Ole Miss students were synthetic opioids, not natural kratom, amid pending toxicology.
story: Mac Haddow, senior fellow on public policy at the American Kratom Association, shares his viewpoint on the potential mischaracterization of kratom during the investigation into two students who attended the University of Mississippi.
Amid the ongoing investigation into the deaths of two Ole Miss students, representatives of the kratom industry are speaking out about how the product may have been mischaracterized.
Court documents show that Aidan Hamilton, 18, and Robert Strang, 20, were discovered dead on Sept. 21 at separate locations.
Initial reports stated that products described as "packaged kratom" or "synthetic kratom" were found near both students.
In a Sept. 30 statement, however, investigators said only that "packaging associated with kratom-related products" had been recovered at both locations.
WHAT IS KRATOM? RISKS OF POPULAR SUBSTANCE REVEALED AFTER COLLEGE STUDENTS' DEATHS

"During the investigations, packaging associated with kratom-related products was discovered at both locations," Lafayette County Metro Narcotics, a department in the sheriff's office, said in the statement Wednesday.
Toxicology results from the medical examiner are still pending.

Amid the ongoing investigation into the deaths of two Ole Miss students, representatives of the kratom industry are speaking out about how the product may have been mischaracterized. (American Kratom Association)
Packaging found near both students bears the name Modus, according to court documents.
The affidavit describes the tablets as Smax Pseudo-DHM, and lists pseudoindoxyl and MGM-15(DHM) among the ingredients on the pack found near Hamilton.

Mac Haddow, senior fellow on public policy at the American Kratom Association in Virginia, spoke with Fox News Digital Thursday about the initial reports of packaged kratom at the two locations where the students were discovered.
OLE MISS NAMES STUDENTS FOUND DEAD AS OFFICIAL ADDRESSES POTENTIAL FOR FOUL PLAY

"We were deeply concerned with that characterization because it is highly unlikely, if not statistically improbable, that a natural kratom leaf product would be the cause of two deaths independently, let alone one," he said.

After attempting to contact the Oxford Police Department, Haddow said the association held a news conference in Oxford asking for clarification on why officials would have disclosed a packaged kratom product.

"It is highly unlikely, if not statistically improbable, that a natural kratom leaf product would be the cause of two deaths independently, let alone one," a representative of the American Kratom Association told Fox News Digital.   (iStock)
The clarification showed that the products recovered were "chemically manipulated opioids, not kratom," Haddow added.

"We are grateful for the clarification because what they have told us and disclosed is that these, in fact, were highly synthetic and importantly controlled substances under the Federal Controlled Substances Act," he said.
HEAVY DRINKING SURGES AMONG AMERICANS IN ONE AGE GROUP AS OTHER GENERATIONS CUT BACK
"Those products never should have been on the market in the first place in those locations."
The Mississippi Kratom Consumer Protection Act (KCPA) is a state law that regulates the sale of kratom rather than banning it.
The focus of the American Kratom Association is on protecting the natural leaf and banning synthetic products, the group said.  (American Kratom Association)
The law establishes standards for who may sell kratom, which products are permitted and how they must be labeled, while prohibiting certain adulterated or high-potency products.
"Why were they not enforcing it?" Haddow questioned.
Natural vs synthetic
According to Haddow, natural kratom leaves have been used for centuries in Southeast Asia.
He argued there have been no published reports of deaths linked to traditional leaf use in the region, although medical literature does describe some adverse effects associated with long-term use.

In 2012, the FDA issued an import alert on kratom products, and the DEA sought to temporarily classify kratom's primary alkaloids as Schedule I substances in 2016 before withdrawing the proposal after public comment. (American Kratom Association)

Haddow said he believes kratom first spread in the U.S. after the Vietnam War, when returning soldiers and Southeast Asian immigrants brought it back from the region. However, researchers note that this origin story remains unsubstantiated in the published literature.
"We need to regulate them, and as we represent consumers, we're going to fight for that."

"And then these amateur chemists got involved and started tinkering with the alkaloids in the natural plant and started to adulterate them, and that appropriately got kratom on the radar of both the DEA and the FDA," he said.

In 2012, the FDA issued an import alert on kratom products, and the DEA sought to temporarily classify kratom's primary alkaloids as Schedule I substances in 2016 before withdrawing the proposal following public comment.

The FDA maintains that kratom has not been approved for any medical use and has warned of some risks, including dependence, contamination and adverse events, while researchers continue to study both the plant and its individual compounds. (Getty Images)
More recently, the agencies have raised concerns about concentrated and chemically modified kratom products, including those containing high levels of 7-hydroxymitragynine (7-OH).
"What these bad actors have done is completely alter the composition of the natural kratom plant," Haddow said.

"They rearranged the molecules. They've chemically synthesized them with high-concentration chlorine and baking soda and other nefarious production methods so that they deliver what is in fact a signature opioid to consumers in the United States."
Calls for stronger enforcement
The association’s focus now is on banning synthetic products and protecting the natural leaf, Haddow said.

"It is improper for any government agency across the country to be blaming natural leaf kratom for any adverse event that is properly attributable to a synthetic opioid," he added, expressing his viewpoint.

"If we were to take coffee and extract caffeine from it and then highly concentrate it to a level in which it is fatal and someone ingested it and died, we wouldn't blame coffee. We would blame the bad actor that took and extracted that caffeine, because caffeine is in its natural form and coffee is not dangerous. The same is true for natural kratom."
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
Haddow said 7-OH products — including pseudoindoxyl and compounds known as MGM-15 and MGM-16 — should not be considered kratom.
"[They] are synthetic opioids, all of which should be enforced by both the federal and local law enforcement agencies," he said.
"We advocate strongly for proper clarification of these dangerous products as opposed to natural kratom, which is literally helping people with their health and wellness and saving lives."
Haddow cited an NIH-led study that is moving forward to evaluate whether purified mitragynine, the main alkaloid in the kratom plant, could help treat opioid use disorder.
Regulation over prohibition
Haddow said the association supports state regulations that require testing, labeling and age restrictions rather than outright bans.

"Make sure the product formulations are safe, make sure the products are labeled correctly and make sure they're age-restricted," he urged. "Twenty-one and up should be the only people who have access to these products.
"We need to regulate them, and as we represent consumers, we're going to fight for that."

The FDA maintains that kratom has not been approved for any medical use and has warned of some risks, including dependence, contamination and adverse events, while researchers continue to study both the plant and its individual compounds.

title: What to know about pentobarbital after death row inmate survives 2 lethal injection doses
summary: A look at pentobarbital reveals why the barbiturate used in Christa Gail Pike's failed lethal injection may not have reached fatal concentrations.
story: A Tennessee execution fails after multiple botched lethal injection attempts on an inmate who survives the ordeal. Steve Harrigan reports on the failed attempts and the governor's decision to halt future executions.

A high-profile execution attempt in Nashville ended in chaos and raised urgent medical questions after Tennessee death row inmate Christa Gail Pike survived two separate doses of lethal pentobarbital, the Associated Press reported.
Pentobarbital is a short-acting barbiturate, according to medical authorities at the National Institutes of Health (NIH).

Historically prescribed as a sedative, anti-seizure medication or sleep aid, pentobarbital enhances the activity of GABA, the brain's primary inhibitory neurotransmitter, slowing activity throughout the central nervous system.
TENNESSEE DEATH ROW INMATE SURVIVES 2 LETHAL INJECTION DOSES IN FAILED EXECUTION ATTEMPT
In clinical medicine, pentobarbital has been used for several purposes, including:

Controlling certain severe or acute seizuresInducing medically managed comas in some patients with severe traumatic brain injury and dangerously elevated intracranial pressureSedating patients before anesthesia or surgery
Controlling certain severe or acute seizures
Inducing medically managed comas in some patients with severe traumatic brain injury and dangerously elevated intracranial pressure
Sedating patients before anesthesia or surgery
Christa Gail Pike is seen during her trial for the murder of Colleen A. Slemmer on March 18, 1996, in Knox County Criminal Court. (USA Today Network via Reuters Connect)
Because newer, safer drugs with lower risks of overdose have largely replaced barbiturates in hospital settings, pentobarbital is now rarely used in routine patient care.

However, it remains a primary agent in veterinary euthanasia and lethal injection protocols across several U.S. states, according to the National Library of Medicine, FDA-approved veterinary drug labeling and the Death Penalty Information Center.
How pentobarbital is used in lethal injections
In a high-dose lethal injection protocol, pentobarbital is administered intravenously in large, ultra-lethal quantities — typically 2.5 to 5 grams (far exceeding clinical therapeutic doses).
JUDGE BLOCKS ALABAMA'S NITROGEN GAS EXECUTION METHOD, RULES IT IS UNCONSTITUTIONALLY CRUEL
When injected directly into a vein, the progression follows three stages, according to medical sources.

Rapid unconsciousness: Within seconds to a few minutes, the drug crosses the blood-brain barrier, inducing surgical anesthesia and loss of consciousness.Respiratory depression: As brainstem activity slows to a halt, the body's ability to breathe automatically is suppressed, causing rapid respiratory arrest.Cardiac arrest: As breathing stops and oxygen levels fall, combined with the drug's depressant effects, the heart eventually stops beating.
Rapid unconsciousness: Within seconds to a few minutes, the drug crosses the blood-brain barrier, inducing surgical anesthesia and loss of consciousness.
Respiratory depression: As brainstem activity slows to a halt, the body's ability to breathe automatically is suppressed, causing rapid respiratory arrest.
Cardiac arrest: As breathing stops and oxygen levels fall, combined with the drug's depressant effects, the heart eventually stops beating.
What happened in the Christa Pike execution?
Pike, 50, who was convicted in the 1995 murder of classmate Colleen Slemmer, was slated to become the first woman executed in Tennessee in more than 200 years.

Media witnesses and defense filings reported that Pike remained conscious and vocal, experienced breathing difficulties, and snored loudly for over 40 minutes after receiving the drug. (Tennessee Department of Correction via AP)
Media witnesses observed her asking if her arm was supposed to feel that way (burning), breathing raggedly, and audibly snoring behind closed curtains over an hour-long span.
The incident prompted Tennessee Gov. Bill Lee to halt all remaining executions in the state pending an independent investigation.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

According to statements from the Tennessee Department of Correction (TDOC), officials administered two doses of pentobarbital, in accordance with the state's established single-drug execution protocol.
State officials maintained that they strictly adhered to the protocol and that the chemical supply was verified.

According to the NIH and Cleveland Clinic, pentobarbital is a short-acting barbiturate used medically as a central nervous system depressant to treat severe seizures and induce medically managed comas. (iStock)
Media witnesses and defense court filings described several problems during the procedure.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER

Difficulty establishing IV access: Defense filings noted that execution staff struggled to establish clear IV lines, a potential point of failure in lethal injections.Failure of the execution: Despite receiving two doses of pentobarbital, Pike continued breathing, occasionally lifting her head and audibly snoring for more than 40 minutes after the second dose.Transfer to a hospital: At 8:53 p.m., prison staff ended the procedure and transferred Pike to an off-site hospital.
Difficulty establishing IV access: Defense filings noted that execution staff struggled to establish clear IV lines, a potential point of failure in lethal injections.
Failure of the execution: Despite receiving two doses of pentobarbital, Pike continued breathing, occasionally lifting her head and audibly snoring for more than 40 minutes after the second dose.
Transfer to a hospital: At 8:53 p.m., prison staff ended the procedure and transferred Pike to an off-site hospital.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
Why do pentobarbital injections fail?
Several possible explanations have been raised in court filings and medical literature, although no cause has been confirmed in Pike’s case.
Medical experts point out that if an IV line slips out of the vein, pentobarbital leaks into surrounding muscle and fat, absorbing too slowly to reach the brain at a lethal concentration. (iStock)

IV infiltration: If an IV line slips out of the vein, the drug can leak into surrounding tissue instead of entering the bloodstream. Absorption is slower, which may delay or prevent the drug from reaching the brain at a concentration sufficient to cause unconsciousness and death.Individual metabolism or tolerance: Differences in liver function, drug metabolism or prior exposure to barbiturates could affect how the body responds to pentobarbital.Drug quality or potency: Because major pharmaceutical manufacturers restrict the use of their drugs in executions, states may obtain pentobarbital from compounding pharmacies, raising questions about its potency, consistency or storage.

Individual metabolism or tolerance: Differences in liver function, drug metabolism or prior exposure to barbiturates could affect how the body responds to pentobarbital.

Drug quality or potency: Because major pharmaceutical manufacturers restrict the use of their drugs in executions, states may obtain pentobarbital from compounding pharmacies, raising questions about its potency, consistency or storage.

As state officials investigate the failed execution, Pike remains under medical observation while legal challenges continue over whether Tennessee may legally attempt a second execution, per reports.

title: Surprising culprit tied to 1 in 8 cancer cases worldwide, major study reveals
summary: A new IARC analysis links 2.3 million cancer cases worldwide to 12 infections, with H. pylori, HPV and hepatitis B leading the global burden.
story: Dr. Joshua Cohen, medical director of the Gynecologic Cancer Program of City of Hope Orange County in Irvine, California, told Fox News Digital that it’s important to seek treatment or preventive mechanisms for certain infections linked to cancer.
About one in eight new cancer cases worldwide in 2024 — 2.3 million cases — have been linked to infections, according to a new analysis from the International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC).

The researchers identified 12 specific infections that were linked to human cancer cases, including Helicobacter pylori (H. pylori), human papillomavirus (HPV), hepatitis B virus (HBV), hepatitis C virus (HCV), Epstein–Barr virus (EBV), Kaposi sarcoma-associated herpesvirus, Schistosoma haematobium, HTLV-1, Opisthorchis viverrini, Clonorchis sinensis, Merkel cell polyomavirus and HIV.
The following five infections contributed to nearly all the global cases.
POPULAR DAILY DRINKING HABIT COULD NEARLY TRIPLE RISK OF DEADLY CANCER, MAJOR STUDY FINDS
H. pylori : ~760,000 casesHPV: ~750,000 casesHBV: ~360,000 casesEBV: ~260,000 casesHCV: ~160,000 cases
H. pylori : ~760,000 cases
HPV: ~750,000 cases
HBV: ~360,000 cases
EBV: ~260,000 cases
HCV: ~160,000 cases
About one in eight new cancer cases worldwide in 2024, 2.3 million cases, were linked to infections, according to a new analysis from the International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC). (iStock)

"The findings underscore the major role that infection control can play in reducing the global cancer burden," said study co-author Dr. Harriet Rumgay, a scientist in the Cancer Surveillance Branch at IARC, in a press release.

"Despite progress in vaccination and screening, infection-related cancers remain a major global challenge, with the burden falling disproportionately on populations in low- and middle-income countries."
CANCER DOCTOR REVEALS 5 HABITS THAT MAY REDUCE DISEASE RISK AND IMPROVE OUTCOMES
The researchers say many of these cancers could have been prevented through vaccination, treatment or screenings.
The study, conducted in France, analyzed cancer data from 2024. The findings were published in The Lancet Oncology on Sept. 28.
Study limitations
The study had several limitations, the researchers acknowledged.
Because the study used population-level estimates rather than tracking individual patients over time, the results depended on the quality of available cancer data in each country.
Additionally, it only included infections already proven to cause cancer, so the total impact could be underestimated.
The researchers identified 12 specific infections that were linked to human cancer cases, including Helicobacter pylori (H. pylori) and human papillomavirus (HPV). (iStock)

"We know that there are certain infections that we are exposed to over our lifetime that may result in an increased risk of certain cancers," Dr. Joshua Cohen, medical director of the Gynecologic Cancer Program of City of Hope Orange County in Irvine, California, told Fox News Digital.
"However, most cancers are not caused by infection."
DOCTORS PUSH NEW BLOOD TESTS FOR COLON CANCER AS CASES SURGE IN YOUNGER ADULTS
HPV is one of the most common drivers of cancers that arise along the rectum, vagina or cervix, as well as the oropharynx (back of the throat), according to Cohen, who was not involved in the study.
"Eighty percent of the population has been exposed to certain types of HPV strains," he said. "About 40,000 people in the U.S. are diagnosed with these cancers each year."
"Most cancers are not caused by infection."
For most people who are exposed to HPV, the body will clear the virus on its own, Cohen said.
"We don't know why some patients' immune systems allow them to clear the HPV infection and some don't."
Another very common cancer, although less so in the U.S., is gastric cancer, he noted, which is linked to H. Pylori, an infection in the stomach.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
"We don't screen everybody for H. pylori in the U.S. — it's more common in other parts of the world, like Southeast Asia."
However, those who have peptic ulcer disease or significant epigastric pain should talk with a gastroenterologist about getting screened and treated for H. pylori, the doctor advised.
Prevention strategies
There are things people can do to reduce the risk of infection-related cancers, according to Cohen.
"As a patient, the most important thing is to think about your health, what you can do to prevent yourself from developing these infections or your family," he said.
The researchers say many of these cancers could have been prevented through vaccination, treatment or screenings. (iStock)
"And if you do have one of these infections, what can you do to reduce your risk of developing a subsequent cancer?"
Cohen emphasized that Americans have access to an HPV vaccination that can help prevent many of these infections.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

"If you’re under the age of 45 and you've not had an HPV vaccination, there is various good safety data that you should get vaccinated," he said. "That will cover, at least in the U.S., most risks regarding oropharyngeal cancers, vaginal cancers, cervical cancers, penile cancers and anal cancers."
"There are steps we can take as doctors to keep you safe and hopefully reduce the risk of developing cancer for those that have had an infection," an oncologist said. (iStock)
The doctor reiterated that developing one of the listed infections doesn’t necessarily mean someone will develop cancer.
"The vast majority of patients who have an HPV infection or H. Pylori, or even hepatitis B or C, are not going to develop cancer," he said.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
But because these infections have been associated with certain cancers, it’s important to seek treatment for them.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Symptoms such as epigastric pain (pain or discomfort in the upper middle part of your abdomen), acid reflux, abnormal vaginal bleeding or pain with swallowing could be related to medical conditions that may be associated with certain infections or cancer, the doctor warned.
"There are steps we can take as doctors to keep you safe and hopefully reduce the risk of developing cancer for those that have had an infection," Cohen added.

title: Rapid weight loss on popular drugs could ‘starve’ the brain, expert warns
summary: Dr. Tommy Wood warns GLP-1 drugs like Ozempic and Wegovy can shrink brain tissue when caloric restriction cuts off vital energy the brain needs.
story: Dr. Tommy Wood, a professor of pediatrics and neuroscience at the University of Washington, shares how GLP-1 weight-loss drugs like Ozempic can affect brain reserve, and why resistance training is critical to protect it.

As GLP-1 weight-loss medications like Ozempic and Wegovy continue to surge in popularity, experts warn that rapid weight loss and severe caloric restriction could deprive the brain of vital energy and nutrients.

Dr. Tommy Wood, a professor of pediatrics and neuroscience at the University of Washington, said the drugs' effects on the brain may depend on whether the body is getting enough energy and nutrients during weight loss.

"The best way to think about this is the spectrum of what we call energy availability," Wood told Fox News Digital at Strong NY, New York City's largest annual fitness and wellness festival. "The brain is your most energy-hungry organ in the body."
POPULAR GLP-1 WEIGHT-LOSS DRUGS LINKED TO POTENTIALLY DEADLY BRAIN DISORDER
According to Wood, brain reserve — the physical amount and integrity of brain tissue — follows a bell-shaped curve relative to the body's energy availability.
Excess energy caused by obesity, high blood sugar and metabolic disease can lower the brain's resilience by damaging blood vessels and contributing to insulin resistance.

As GLP-1 weight-loss medications like Ozempic and Wegovy continue to surge in popularity, experts warn that rapid weight loss and severe caloric restriction could deprive the brain of vital energy and nutrients. (iStock)
In these cases, GLP-1 medications can provide cognitive benefits by lowering blood pressure and improving blood sugar control.

However, Wood noted that the lower end of the energy spectrum poses its own structural risks to the brain. Because the brain relies heavily on continuous fuel, extreme caloric deficits can force the organ to consume its own tissue.
POPULAR WEIGHT-LOSS DRUGS CAN BECOME AN ‘ATOMIC BOMB’ AT HIGH DOSES, DOCTOR WARNS

"There was a study that looked at the brains of people who ran a marathon ... because the marathon is so energy-intensive, the white matter in the brain actually shrank during a marathon because the brain didn't have enough energy … so it was eating its own white matter," Wood said, noting that the participants' brains recovered after resting and refueling.
"It just shows that the brain is really energy-hungry, and it will decrease its size if it's not getting enough energy."
If people aren't eating enough, they're not getting the nutrients that are critical for brain health, according to Wood. (iStock)
Muscle quality
Concerns about lean muscle loss when taking GLP-1 medications are often nuanced, Wood said. Some of the early "lean mass" that's lost is actually fat that had built up inside the muscles.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
"So technically, your muscles get smaller, but you don't get weaker," he told Fox News Digital. "And the quality and functioning of your muscles actually gets better."
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

However, risks arise when individuals taking GLP-1 medications drastically reduce their food intake for extended periods. Chronic under-eating can deprive the central nervous system of essential structural nutrients, Wood warned.
Ensuring adequate intake of core neuro-nutrients — including B vitamins (B12, folate, B6), vitamin D, iron and omega-3 fatty acids — prevents long-term cognitive impairment. (iStock)

"It is possible that you can end up going too far," he said. "If you're not eating enough, you're not getting the nutrients that are critical for the brain. So you're not getting in enough omega-3 fats, which we know are really important. You're not getting enough iron and protein and all those kinds of things."
Protecting the brain during weight loss

To safeguard brain health while losing weight, Wood recommends pairing weight-loss regimens with resistance training twice a week to maintain functional muscle mass and to stimulate brain growth factors.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

Additionally, ensuring adequate intake of core "neuro-nutrients" — including B vitamins (B12, folate, B6), vitamin D, iron and omega-3 fatty acids — prevents long-term cognitive impairment, according to Wood.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"For most people, I think it's going to be beneficial to start, but you just need to make sure that you don't push it too far, that you're now getting enough of everything that the brain needs," he advised.
Khloe Quill is a lifestyle writer with Fox News Digital. She and the lifestyle team cover a range of story topics including food and drink, travel, and health.

title: Heavy drinking surges among Americans in one age group as other generations cut back
summary: Adults ages 50 to 64 saw heavy drinking surge more than 36% since 2018, even as overall U.S. alcohol use finally began to decline post-pandemic.
story: Dr. Chris Tuell, clinical director of addiction services at the University of Cincinnati College of Medicine, discusses why alcohol poses higher risks to people as they age, and shares tips for moderating intake.

New research shows that U.S. alcohol use has declined for the first time since the COVID-19 pandemic, but drinking remains above pre-pandemic levels — with one particular group showing a sharp increase in heavy intake.

A study led by the University of Southern California/Keck Medicine found that among adults ages 50 to 64, alcohol use increased by nearly 4% from 2018 to 2024, while heavy drinking increased by more than 36%.
Across all age groups, alcohol use declined by nearly 2%, and heavy drinking declined by more than 8% from 2022 to 2024. However, overall alcohol use remained above pre-pandemic levels.
BEER, WINE OR LIQUOR? MASSIVE STUDY REVEALS WHICH WAS LINKED TO LOWER DEATH RISK
Among Gen Z adults, alcohol use declined by more than 5%. Millennials drank approximately 17% less from 2022 to 2024.

The findings, which were published on Sept. 21 in Annals of Internal Medicine, were based on self-reported data from the National Health Interview Survey, which included 114,352 U.S. adults from 2018 to 2024.

A study led by the University of Southern California/Keck Medicine found that among adults ages 50 to 64, alcohol use increased by nearly 4% from 2018 to 2024, while heavy drinking increased by more than 36%. (iStock)
Heavy drinking was defined as five or more drinks per day or 15 or more drinks per week for men within the preceding 12 months and at least four daily drinks or eight weekly drinks for women.
Men were found to have a larger alcohol decline than women (2.4% vs. 1.1%), but women had a larger reduction in heavy drinking (9%) compared to men (7.7%).
ALCOHOL TIED TO SURPRISING CANCER DEATH PATTERN IN ADULTS UNDER 55, RESEARCHERS FIND

"Women’s heavy drinking rose more than men's during the pandemic and is still about 13% above where it was in 2018," lead study author Brian P. Lee, M.D., associate professor of medicine at the Keck School of Medicine of USC, told Fox News Digital. "Women develop liver damage at lower levels of drinking than men, so that number carries more weight than it looks."
The study was funded in part by the National Institute on Alcohol Abuse and Alcoholism and the National Institutes of Health.
Men were found to have a larger alcohol decline than women (2.4% vs. 1.1%), but women had a larger reduction in heavy drinking (9%) compared to men (7.7%). (iStock)
Study limitations
The chief limitation of the study is that people reported their own levels of drinking, which tend to run low, according to Lee.

"It also can't tell us why drinking changed, only that it did," he told Fox News Digital. "And we have two years of decline after four years of increases, so I'd describe this as a promising turn rather than an established trend."
The researchers also did not investigate the reasons younger adults reduced alcohol consumption.
"Women develop liver damage at lower levels of drinking than men, so that number carries more weight than it looks."
Potential reasons older adults are drinking more
Dr. Chris Tuell, clinical director of addiction services at the University of Cincinnati College of Medicine, said many factors may contribute to the increased rate of drinking among older adults.
"As we approach our 50s and 60s, we start reflecting on our lives, and changes start to happen," Tuell, who was not involved in the study, told Fox News Digital.
The loneliness epidemic in the U.S., and the fact that people are more "polarized" and "disconnected," may also come into play, according to an addiction expert. (iStock)
The loneliness epidemic in the U.S., and the fact that people are more "polarized" and "disconnected," may also come into play, according to Tuell.
Grief and loss may also lead to increased drinking as people seek a way to escape or cope with the loss of friends and family members.

"One out of four people will experience some mental health issue … depression, anxiety, loss, grief — these are real things that are impacting people," Tuell said. "And it's at a time where a person might feel very vulnerable."
BRAD PITT SAYS HE CAN DRINK IN ‘RESTRAINED MANNER’ AFTER 7 SOBER YEARS, BUT EXPERT RAISES RED FLAG
As people age, there may also be increased issues related to chronic pain and medical issues, resulting in reduced function.
"Now I have these aches and pains, or maybe I'm diagnosed with something more serious," Tuell said as an example. "So that becomes a problem that I now have to deal with."
Grief and loss may also lead to increased drinking as people seek a way to escape or cope with the loss of friends and family members. (iStock)
Many aging adults are also approaching retirement age, which can result in a loss of structure and change the identity they’ve had for decades, the expert noted.

"I wake up and something I've done every day for many, many years is no longer happening. So I'm more bored. What do I do with my time? This is unfortunately a perfect storm for things like substance use."
Risks of alcohol for older adults
As older adults experience body changes, they don't metabolize alcohol the same way they once did, Tuell noted.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
"What I used to drink maybe five years ago … that same amount now can affect me differently, because I'm not metabolizing it like I used to," he said.
Women are especially impacted by alcohol, Tuell said, likely because they may have less body fat and don't have as much water in their bodies.
For those who are over 50 and drinking more than they did before 2020, the lead researcher recommends asking a doctor about liver health, "even if nothing feels wrong." (iStock)
Lee noted that while alcohol doesn't harm everyone equally, the risk starts at low levels and goes up with every additional drink.
"There isn't a level the evidence shows to be safe."
Red flags
To determine whether someone has a problem with alcohol, Tuell recommends using the "three Cs."

Control: "Is there a loss of control? I can't manage this behavior any longer."Compulsive: "I can’t stop doing it. I continue to do it despite the negative consequences. Knowing that I could lose my job, I could lose my marriage, I could lose lots of things in my life, I do it anyway."Continued use despite adverse consequences: "I can't stop thinking about it — it might be the first thing I think about when I wake up in the morning or the last thing I think about when I go to bed."
Control: "Is there a loss of control? I can't manage this behavior any longer."

Compulsive: "I can’t stop doing it. I continue to do it despite the negative consequences. Knowing that I could lose my job, I could lose my marriage, I could lose lots of things in my life, I do it anyway."

Continued use despite adverse consequences: "I can't stop thinking about it — it might be the first thing I think about when I wake up in the morning or the last thing I think about when I go to bed."
Alcohol can still be problematic even if someone doesn’t have an addiction, Tuell noted.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
For example, they might drink more than they should, to the point where they get a hangover or put themselves at risk.
"Maybe it's impacting my interactions with other people, interpersonal relationships, hobbies, interests," he said. "Maybe it's affecting my sleep."
In a normal sleep pattern, people go through a cycle four to five times per night, but when they drink, it's more like two to three times, the expert said. (iStock)

In a normal sleep pattern, people go through a cycle four to five times per night, but when they drink, it's more like two to three times, Tuell said. "So, we're not getting good rest during that period."
It’s never too late to seek help with alcohol dependency, he pointed out.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

"I've treated people in their 80s who still have a lot of life left," Tuell said, pointing out that Americans are living longer. "So we're aging, we're getting older, and there are a lot of life changes happening … physically, emotionally, psychologically."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
For those who are over 50 and drinking more than they did before 2020, Lee recommends asking a doctor about liver health, "even if nothing feels wrong."

"There are clear increases in cancer and liver risk with alcohol, even at low levels," he warned. "Even advanced liver disease might have no symptoms, and the earlier alcohol-related liver damage is caught, the more of it can be undone."
