title: Shooting near Baltimore youth football event leaves 12-year-old girl dead, 3 adults wounded
summary: A parking dispute near a youth football event at Leon Day Park in Baltimore turned deadly when two men allegedly opened fire on each other, killing a 12-year-old girl in the crossfire.
story: Police responded to Leon Day Park in Baltimore after gunfire erupted during a youth football game, leaving multiple people shot. (WBFF)
A 12-year-old girl was killed and three adults were wounded after two gunmen allegedly opened fire during a dispute near a youth football game in Baltimore, Maryland, authorities said Saturday.

The preteen girl was apparently caught in the crossfire at Leon Day Park, where a youth football league was holding its homecoming event, Baltimore Police Commissioner Richard Worley said during a news conference.
The two men are believed to have been in a dispute that started over a parking space, according to Worley.
"What we know is that there was some type of argument between two cowards, and of course, they both opened fire on each other," Worley said.
PANTHERS GREAT JONATHAN STEWART EXPLAINS WHY YOUTH SPORTS MATTER FAR BEYOND THE FIELD
A 12-year-old girl was killed and three adults were wounded after gunfire erupted near a youth football game at Leon Day Park in Baltimore, authorities said. (Baltimore Police Department)
"In the crossfire, a 12-year-old little girl who was probably down there watching football was shot and killed," he added.
As of Saturday evening, police said they were searching for at least two suspects, whom authorities described as adult men. No arrests had been announced as of late Saturday night.
Baltimore police told Fox News Digital that officers responded to the 1200 block of North Franklintown Road at approximately 6:15 p.m. after receiving multiple reports of gunfire.
Officers found a 25-year-old woman suffering from an apparent gunshot wound and the 12-year-old girl, who was transported to a hospital but later pronounced dead.
LEXINGTON, KENTUCKY PARK SHOOTING KILLS 1, INJURES 4 DURING LIVE BAND PERFORMANCE
Baltimore homicide detectives are investigating a shooting that authorities said left a 12-year-old girl dead and three other victims in stable condition. (Baltimore Police)
A 28-year-old man and a 23-year-old man separately walked into area hospitals seeking treatment for gunshot wounds, police said.
All three surviving victims were listed in stable condition.
Baltimore Mayor Brandon Scott gave an emotionally charged reaction to the incident, which he said unfolded because two adults couldn't resolve an argument without guns.
"Two grown men got into an argument and now a 12-year-old is gone," he said.
AT LEAST 3 DEAD, 23 WOUNDED IN SEPARATE MASS SHOOTINGS LESS THAN 15 MINUTES APART
A youth football homecoming event was underway at Leon Day Park in Baltimore on Oct. 3, 2026, when gunfire erupted, leaving a 12-year-old girl dead, according to city officials. (WBFF)
"What happened out here today is one of the most disgusting things I've ever seen in my life," Scott added.
Scott said the girl's death would have a profound impact on the community before offering his condolences to her family.
"We're never gonna see her full potential," he said. "Her family's gonna be hurting for this for the rest of their life. Her classmates are going to be hurting, her community's going to be hurting."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Anyone with information is asked to call homicide detectives at 410-396-2100 or Metro Crime Stoppers at 1-866-7LOCKUP. Anonymous tips can also be submitted through Metro Crime Stoppers of Maryland.

title: Texas mother facing capital murder charges after allegedly shooting her two sons to death
summary: Colleen Nichole Lemmon allegedly told officers she shot both her sons at their Waxahachie home before deputies found her with self-inflicted injuries.
story: Fox News anchor Martha MacCallum reports new details on the case of Lindsay Clancy, a Massachusetts mother suspected of murdering her three children, on 'The Story.'
A Texas mother is facing capital murder charges after allegedly shooting her two sons before appearing to harm herself, authorities said.
Colleen Nichole Lemmon, 42, was taken into custody and charged with two counts of capital murder, according to the Ellis County Sheriff's Office.
Authorities said they received a call about an "unknown emergency" just before 4:15 a.m. Thursday on Big Sky Drive in Waxahachie.
Upon arriving at the scene, deputies discovered two male victims with gunshot wounds inside the residence.
ILLINOIS MOTHER CHARGED WITH MURDER IN DEATH OF 2-YEAR-OLD SON IN CASE DRAWING COMPARISONS TO LINDSAY CLANCY
Colleen Nichole Lemmon, 42, was arrested after authorities said her two sons were fatally shot at a home in Waxahachie, Texas. (Ellis County Sheriff's Office)
Christopher Scott Pitre, 21, was pronounced dead at the scene. The second victim, a 15-year-old boy, was taken to a hospital in critical condition, where he later died.
Deputies said they also found Lemmon suffering from non-life-threatening injuries.
Evidence recovered during the investigation gave law enforcement probable cause to believe Lemmon was responsible for shooting both of her children.
DAYS AFTER LINDSAY CLANCY MISTRIAL, ANOTHER MASSACHUSETTS MOM ACCUSED OF KILLING HER CHILDREN SEEKS FREEDOM
Colleen Nichole Lemmon, 42, is charged with two counts of capital murder in connection with the shooting deaths of her two sons in Waxahachie, Texas, authorities said. (Ellis County Sheriff's Office)
Deputies found Lemmon covered in blood with what appeared to be self-inflicted lacerations on her wrists and a handgun nearby, according to an arrest affidavit obtained by FOX 4.
Lemmon allegedly told officers, "I shot both my kids."
She was arrested and transported to a local hospital for treatment, authorities said.
Scott Pitre, the boys' father, told NBC 5 that his younger son had recently celebrated his 15th birthday. He said he wants justice for his sons.
LINDSAY CLANCY'S THREE CHILD VICTIMS FORGOTTEN AMID CROWDS OF SUPPORT: MOTHER OF SIX
The Ellis County Sheriff's Office is investigating the fatal shootings of two brothers at a home in Waxahachie, Texas. (Google Maps)
Ida Brown, a neighbor, described the killings as "heartbreaking."
"It's heartbreaking, and I'm praying for them," she told FOX 4.
Sheriff Brad Norman offered his condolences to the family.

"My deepest sympathies go out to the victims' father, family members, and loved ones involved in this tragic incident," Norman said in a statement. "They will remain in our prayers during this difficult time."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Lemmon is being held on a $2.5 million bond.
Michael Sinkewicz is a writer for Fox News Digital. Story tips can be sent to michael.sinkewicz@fox.com

title: Cornell president says university 'must do better' on handling of sexual assault allegations
summary: Cornell University President Michael Kotlikoff said the university "must do better" after questions arose over its handling of fraternity sexual assault claims.
story: Cornell University President Michael Kotlikoff delivers remarks following an alleged gang rape involving students. (Cornell University)

Cornell University President Michael Kotlikoff said Saturday that the institution "must do better" as it faces questions over its response to sexual assault allegations involving seven former fraternity brothers.

"What happened to Jane Doe in 2024 is deeply disturbing and will weigh heavily on our community for years to come. My heart aches when I think of what she experienced," Kotlikoff said in a video statement to the Cornell community.

Kotlikoff said the case raises questions about sexual assault, campus party culture, alcohol and drug abuse on the Ithaca, New York, campus, as well as the investigation conducted after the allegations were reported.

"I want to acknowledge something that can be difficult for an institution to say we don't have all the answers, but we are committed to investigating and finding the answers our community deserves. I believe we as an administration, and we as a community must do better," Kotlikoff said.
INSIDE EXPLOSIVE CORNELL RAPE ALLEGATIONS: 7 MEN ACCUSED, CONFLICTING ACCOUNTS AND A POLITICAL FIRESTORM
Kotlikoff said the case raises questions about sexual assault and campus party culture. (Matt Burkhartt/Getty Images, File)

Kotlikoff welcomed an independent review by an outside law firm into Cornell's handling of the case and said the university supports Gov. Kathy Hochul's decision to turn the criminal investigation over to New York Attorney General Letitia James.
He said Cornell would not wait for those reviews to conclude before making changes to prevention and education, student support, mental health and substance use resources and investigative processes.

"We will act," Kotlikoff said.Jane Doe alleges in a lawsuit that seven former Chi Phi fraternity brothers drugged and sexually assaulted her during an October 2024 night at the fraternity house. Doe was a 20-year-old Cornell undergraduate at the time.
CORNELL RAPE ALLEGATIONS PROMPT NY ATTORNEY GENERAL LETITIA JAMES TO OPEN ‘ACTIVE CRIMINAL INVESTIGATION’
Cornell University in Ithaca, N.Y., is facing renewed scrutiny over its handling of sexual assault allegations involving seven former fraternity brothers. (TW Farlow/Getty Images, File)
The men have denied wrongdoing, with some maintaining the sexual activity was consensual and others denying they participated. No criminal charges have been filed against the seven men.
Doe filed a 101-page lawsuit last month accusing the former fraternity members of sexual assault and rape and naming Cornell and other entities.

The case came under renewed scrutiny after Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten said his office had not received the full transcript of Doe's November 2024 interview with Cornell University Police before prosecutors initially declined to pursue charges.

Van Houten reopened the investigation before Hochul appointed the Office of the Attorney General as special prosecutor. James said Friday that her office was conducting an "active criminal investigation."
CORNELL SEXUAL ASSAULT CASE REVIVES SCRUTINY OF A LITTLE-KNOWN NEW YORK LAW ON INTOXICATED VICTIMS

The Chi Phi fraternity house at Cornell University, left, and New York Gov. Kathy Hochul with Attorney General Letitia James, right. James has opened an active criminal investigation into sexual assault allegations stemming from an October 2024 incident at the fraternity house. (Spencer Platt/Getty Images)
Kotlikoff also addressed frustration over Cornell's communication about its response to the allegations and said the university would make a greater effort to be transparent.

"There are real legal and privacy limits on what we can say, but we will make a greater effort to explain what we can to provide context about the actions Cornell has taken and to be more transparent," Kotlikoff said.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Kotlikoff said Cornell would also reexamine the role of fraternities and sororities on campus and support efforts to change New York's sexual assault laws.
"You have my commitment that this will not be a moment that passes," Kotlikoff said.
Fox News Digital's Michael Dorgan contributed to this report.
Brittany Miller is a Fox News Digital breaking news writer and former Independent reporter who graduated from Syracuse University in 2023.

title: South Carolina mom couldn't remember last time she fed 2 daughters before they were found dead: affidavits
summary: Justine Marie May allegedly told South Carolina detectives the prior two weeks were a "blur" before deputies found both daughters dead in their home.
story: Fox News Flash top headlines are here. Check out what's clicking on FoxNews.com.

A South Carolina mother told investigators she could not remember the last time she gave her two young daughters food or something to drink before deputies found both children dead inside their home, according to affidavits reviewed by Fox News Digital.
Justine Marie May, 31, faces two counts of homicide by child abuse in connection with the Sept. 29 deaths of her daughters at the family's home in Ladson, outside Charleston, court documents show.
Charleston County Sheriff's Office deputies responding to a welfare check allegedly encountered May outside the home crying and "speaking incoherently," according to the affidavits.
OHIO MOM OF 16 CRADLES STOMACH IN COURT, PLEADS NOT GUILTY IN SEVERE ABUSE CASE INVOLVING OWN CHILDREN
Justine Marie May, 31, faces two counts of homicide by child abuse in connection with the deaths of her two young daughters in Ladson, S.C. (Charleston County Sheriff's Office)
Deputies entered the home to check on the children and found both dead, the documents state.
May told detectives the previous two weeks had been a "blur" and that she could not remember when she last fed the children or gave them something to drink, according to the affidavits.

She allegedly told investigators she believed the children died because they did not eat and acknowledged that not feeding them was neglectful, the documents state. May also said she had been the only person at the home and the children's sole caregiver during the previous few weeks.FLORIDA COUPLE ALLEGEDLY HELD FOUR CHILDREN IN TRACTOR-TRAILER CAB FOR NEARLY SIX YEARS
The Charleston County Sheriff's Office of Professional Standards in South Carolina is conducting an internal review of the agency's response. (Google Maps)
The affidavits describe the children as approximately 1½ and 2½ years old at the time of their deaths.
Investigators accused May of showing "extreme indifference for human life" by failing to provide her children with basic sustenance, which they alleged was a "main contributor to their death."
Separate arrest warrants were issued for each child, charging May with homicide by child abuse under South Carolina law.
‘THIS IS REAL BAD’: 911 CALL REVEALS FRANTIC MOMENTS AFTER AUTISTIC DAUGHTER, 5, VANISHED IN SOUTH CAROLINA

A stock image of police emergency lights. The Charleston County Sheriff’s Office is investigating the deaths of two young girls whose mother, Justine Marie May, faces two counts of homicide by child abuse. (iStock)

The Charleston County Sheriff's Office said deputies had made separate contact with May and the children twice in August and three times in September and reported seeing no obvious signs of concern during those encounters, according to published reports.
Their last reported visit while the children were alive was Sept. 20.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

The Charleston County Sheriff's Office of Professional Standards is conducting an internal review of the agency's response, while the South Carolina Law Enforcement Division's Special Victims Unit and the Department of Child Fatalities are assisting in the investigation, according to published reports.

May was booked into the Charleston County jail on Sept. 29 and remained in custody as of Friday, according to online jail records reviewed by Fox News Digital. The records list two homicide by child abuse charges.
Brittany Miller is a Fox News Digital breaking news writer and former Independent reporter who graduated from Syracuse University in 2023.

title: Trump's attempted assassin sent mysterious texts about 3D printer leading up to Butler, Pa, shooting: report
summary: FBI records obtained by Judicial Watch reveal Thomas Matthew Crooks sent cryptic coded texts and took drone photos of Pittsburgh stadiums before the attack
story: Former Deputy Assistant Attorney General John Yoo discusses FBI documents detailing the background and actions of Thomas Crooks before his alleged assassination attempt on President Donald Trump at a rally in Butler, Pa., on ‘The Will Cain Show.’

Thomas Matthew Crooks, the shooter in the assassination attempt at President Donald Trump's Butler, Pennsylvania, rally July 13, 2024, sent a series of strangely coded text messages in the months leading up to the shooting, according to records obtained by Judicial Watch.
"Did you 3D print the parts?" an individual the FBI described as an "unknown contact" messaged Crooks Feb. 9, 2023.
"Yes, except for the fan blades," Crooks responded.
"Woah that looks cool," the unknown contact replied to Crooks, also asking about the "parts" in response to a Crooks message, which the FBI redacted.
GOP LAWMAKERS BLINDSIDED BY NEW REVELATIONS ABOUT TRUMP BUTLER SHOOTER: 'AWFULLY STRANGE'

Thomas Matthew Crooks was a 20-year-old from Bethel Park, Pa., who attempted to assassinate former President Donald Trump during a 2024 campaign rally before being shot and killed by Secret Service agents. (Obtained by Fox News Digital)
ATTEMPTED TRUMP ASSASSIN THOMAS CROOKS’ BEHAVIOR REVEALED ‘RED FLAGS’ BEFORE ATTACK: FORMER FBI AGENT
Another series of messages between Crooks and a redacted second party display a series of odd one- or two-word messages Crooks sent the contact between May 21, 2023, and Jan. 3, 2024.
"Hello … Hello red …Hello red … Hdudhdbdbbd … 7888ejdj … Yolo … Ddodjjf … 890 … Hdjd … Djdj … red … Yup red … Hello … Jhhhuuh … Hhdj … Jjjjjjjjjjjj … Hello red … Red red," Crooks' messages said.
The FBI redacted any potential response from the other party, according to the documents.
Other information Judicial Watch received from the FBI documents included a notification from shipping company DHL about a package Crooks received from Hong Kong.
ATTEMPTED TRUMP ASSASSIN THOMAS CROOKS USED 'BOB DOLE' ALIAS BEFORE ANONYMOUS DONOR PAID FOR CREMATION: DOCS

The document release also included 40 drone photos Crooks took between Feb. 6, 2024, and Feb. 27, 2024, which included photos of PNC Park and Acrisure Stadium, where the MLB's Pittsburgh Pirates and the NFL's Pittsburgh Steelers play, respectively.

Crooks' affinity for 3D printing had been previously reported by the New York Post after the outlet reviewed a series of documents obtained by Senate Judiciary Committee Chairman Sen. Chuck Grassley, R-Iowa.
UKRAINIAN NATIONAL WHO COMPLETED AIR FORCE OFFICER TRAINING CONVICTED IN GHOST GUN 3D PRINTING OPERATION
Crooks had previously attempted to use his 3D printer to create a Glock 19 handgun, his father, Matthew Crooks, told investigators, according to the documents obtained by Grassley.
"Using carbon fiber plastic, a dryer and a toaster oven, Thomas did once create a Glock 19," Matthew Crooks told investigators.

The family of Thomas Crooks leaves the house in Bethel Park, Pa. Aug. 1, 2024. Crooks died while attempting to assassinate President Donald Trump in Butler July 13, 2024. (Derek Shook for Fox News Digital)
BLUE STATE GOVERNORS JOIN GUN-GRABBING EFFORTS BY TARGETING GLOCK PISTOLS
But, fearing the gun would explode, Matthew Crooks forbade his son from using it, according to records obtained by the Post.

Crooks' assassination attempt on candidate Donald Trump, while unsuccessful in killing Trump, resulted in the deaths of two civilians. Corey Comperatore, a 50-year-old fire chief, died immediately while shielding his family from bullets.
TWO YEARS AFTER BUTLER, THREATS AGAINST TRUMP KEEP ASSASSINATION ATTEMPT IN SHARP FOCUS

Republican presidential candidate Donald Trump is rushed offstage by U.S. Secret Service agents after being grazed by a bullet during a rally on July 13, 2024, in Butler, Pa. (Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images)
James Copenhaver, a 76-year-old veteran, was shot in the triceps and the midsection, sustaining injuries to vital organs, including his kidneys and colon.
Though Copenhaver was released from the hospital a week after the shooting, he dealt with complications from the injuries in the ensuing years.
On Sept. 23, 2026, he died due to those complications.
James Copenhaver prior to an interview in Pittsburgh, Pa., July 8, 2025. (David Dee Delgado for Fox News Digital)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
"These latest records reveal more pieces of the puzzle surrounding Thomas Crooks," Judicial Watch President Tom Fitton said in a statement.

"The FBI should stop the slow drip of heavily redacted records and immediately provide the full investigative record — especially since the death last week of James Copenhaver, who was severely injured from being shot during the assassination attempt on President Trump."

title: Coast Guard finds debris field off Nantucket after Boston-bound medevac plane vanishes with 6 on board
summary: A Gulfstream G100 with 6 people on board vanished en route to Boston from Bermuda on Saturday as search crews deploy off Nantucket to conduct a search. Officials said a debris field has been found.
story: Fox News correspondent CB Cotton discusses the Coast Guard’s assistance in the search for a jet missing off the coast of Nantucket on ‘Fox Report.’

U.S. Coast Guard search crews located a debris field off the Nantucket coast that has been confirmed to be associated with a medevac flight with six people on board that disappeared Saturday morning while en route to Boston from Bermuda.

Crews are continuing to search for potential survivors, and the Coast Guard cutter William Sparling will continue search efforts throughout the night. The Coast Guard said it would hold a news conference Sunday morning.

Authorities are searching for the Gulfstream G100, a twin-engine, midsize jet, off Nantucket. Both air and surface crews have been deployed to the area, according to the Coast Guard Northeast District.
The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) reported losing contact with the aircraft early Saturday, the Coast Guard said.
FRANTIC SEARCH UNDERWAY FOR CREW AFTER BOEING 737 WRECKAGE FOUND BY OFFICIALS
U.S. Coast Guard crews search off the Nantucket coast for a medevac plane believed to have crashed en route to Boston from Bermuda, Saturday. (U.S. Coast Guard)
Earlier Saturday, the FAA issued a statement that said it is "coordinating with the Rescue Coordination Center and the U.S. Coast Guard to locate the aircraft."
According to data from FlightAware, the plane took off from Bermuda L. F. Wade International Airport at 11:41 p.m. ET.
The FAA told Fox News Digital it issued a Search and Rescue Alert Notice at about 1:20 a.m. ET.
The Massachusetts Port Authority (Massport), which operates the state's three major airports, confirmed that the aircraft did not arrive at Boston Logan International Airport as scheduled.
"Our thoughts are with those on board and their loved ones as the search continues," the agency said.
SKYDIVERS WATCH PLANE VANISH FROM SIGHT, MAKE SPLIT-SECOND DECISION TO JUMP
Nantucket harbormaster and police search the south shore of the island Saturday, after a Boston-bound plane reportedly vanished off the island. (Nantucket Current)
The Canadian-registered aircraft is owned by Latitude Air Ambulance, the company confirmed to Fox News Digital, adding that it was a medevac flight.
Two Canadian pilots, two medical workers, one patient and a patient's companion were on board.
Latitude Air Ambulance is a medical transport company that brings patients home from around the world when they require specialized care.
Latitude Air Ambulance said the flight was supposed to take about two hours.
The National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) told Fox News Digital that it is currently gathering information and declined to provide an update on the situation.
A Coast Guard HC-130 Hercules is among the assets searching for the plane. (U.S. Coast Guard, File)

"My thoughts are with the six people aboard the missing air ambulance traveling from Bermuda to Boston, and their families," Bermuda's Premier David Burt said in a statement. "Government has contacted the family and US search and rescue authorities. We are praying that everyone will be found safe."
The plane plummeted from 24,000 feet to 11,000 feet in just three minutes at around 1 a.m., according to data from FlightAware.

Skyport, the company that manages the airport in Bermuda, confirmed that a "Canadian-registered air ambulance departed L. F. Wade International Airport for Boston at approximately 12:41 am on Saturday, October 3, 2026, with six souls on board, including four crew members and two passengers."

"The U.S. Federal Aviation Administration has advised that air traffic controllers lost contact with the aircraft off the coast of Nantucket Island, Massachusetts, and a search is currently underway. Skyport has no further information to provide at this time," the company added.
Waters off the Nantucket coast, where the Coast Guard is searching for a missing plane. (Stan Grossfeld/The Boston Globe via Getty Images, File)

title: ‘Tinder Swindler’ romance fraudster promises ‘safe’ dating app, using intel from con man playbook
summary: Simon Leviev, the notorious "Tinder Swindler" who was born Shimon Hayut, says his new Safe Love dating app will use identity verification to prevent the fraud he once committed.
story: ‘Outnumbered’ panelists discuss the single woman who went viral for creating a Google Form husband application to find a spouse.
Deception, scams and cases of false identity.
These are common risks in online dating that Simon Leviev said he can prevent with his soon-to-be released dating app, Safe Love.
He knows how fraudsters commit those deceptions. He was one of them.

Leviev, who was born Shimon Yehuda Hayut, gained prominence as the "Tinder Swindler" because of his romance fraud schemes. The 36-year-old made a lavish income extorting money from women he met online.
VICTIMS OF NETFLIX DOC'S ALLEGED ‘TINDER SWINDLER’ HAVE UNITED FOR THIS REASON: ‘A BIG F--- YOU TO HIM'
Simon Leviev, born Shimon Hayut, gained prominence as the "Tinder Swindler" because of his romance fraud schemes. (Simon Leviev)
In 2015 and 2019, he was convicted of fraud, theft and forgery charges in Israel and Finland, he confirmed to Fox News Digital in a video conference interview.

He served time in Finland from September 2015 until March 2017, he said. He was arrested in Israel in 2011 and 2017 for the same case. And in June 2019, he was extradited from Greece to Israel, where he was jailed until May 2020, he said.

When she tried to escape, they held her down. When she begged for her life, they slashed her with blades. And when she cried, they gagged her with a hair tie. title: FBI's first cyber fugitive on Ten Most Wanted list returns to US after capture in Venezuela
summary: Anibal Alexander Canelon Aguirre, the FBI's first-ever cyber fugitive on its Ten Most Wanted list, pleaded not guilty to ATM jackpotting charges.
story: The Department of Justice charged 17 Iranian nationals for allegedly conducting a massive cyber theft campaign targeting American universities and government agencies. Reporter Alexandria Hoff details how the hackers compromised networks to steal intellectual property since 2013.
A Venezuelan alleged Tren de Aragua leader who became the FBI's first-ever cyber fugitive on its Ten Most Wanted list is back on U.S. soil after being captured overseas last month.
Anibal Alexander Canelon Aguirre, 50, also known as "Prometheus" and "The Engineer," appeared in a Nebraska courtroom Friday to face charges tied to a multimillion-dollar ATM "jackpotting" scheme.
He pleaded not guilty to four federal conspiracy charges during his initial court appearance and will remain detained in Nebraska while awaiting trial, according to the Department of Justice (DOJ).
FBI Director Kash Patel touted Aguirre's return as the 10th Ten Most Wanted fugitive captured since the beginning of the Trump administration and the first cyber fugitive ever placed on the list.
KASH PATEL DEFENDS FBI'S ‘MOST WANTED’ BUSTS AMID MANIPULATION ACCUSATIONS, HIGHLIGHTS 'SUMMER HEAT' SUCCESS

Anibal Alexander Canelon Aguirre, an alleged Tren de Aragua leader and the FBI's first cyber fugitive placed on its Ten Most Wanted list, was captured in Venezuela and returned to the U.S. to face federal charges. (FBI)
"Now he’s back in the United States to face justice," Patel said. "This FBI is running on supercharged horsepower — and there is nowhere on this planet criminals can hide."
Patel said the 10 captures are more than 2½ times the total recorded during the previous four years.
Aguirre was apprehended last month in Venezuela, and Patel subsequently told lawmakers the FBI had captured one of the nation's top fugitives.

The FBI previously told Fox News Digital that Aguirre led "a large international conspiracy to steal millions of dollars from financial institutions in support of the Tren de Aragua, through an ATM jackpotting scheme since at least 2024."
FBI STRIKES BACK AT HACKING GROUP WITH OVERSEAS ARREST OF ALLEGED LEADER
Anibal Alexander Canelon Aguirre, also known as "Prometheus," appears in an FBI mug shot after being charged in a massive alleged ATM jackpotting conspiracy tied to Tren de Aragua. (FBI)

An ATM "jackpotting" attack is a type of cyberattack in which criminals exploit vulnerabilities in an ATM, including through the use of malware, to force the machine to dispense cash, according to the DOJ.
Prosecutors say Canelon Aguirre developed malicious software and was one of the leaders of the alleged ATM jackpotting conspiracy.
The DOJ says the broader ATM jackpotting conspiracy has been linked to Tren de Aragua, which the U.S. has designated as a foreign terrorist organization.
Attorney General Todd Blanche said DOJ has charged nearly 350 alleged TdA members and associates since the designation.
"The capture and arrest of Anibal Alexander Canelon Aguirre marks yet another success for the Homeland Security Task Force and Joint Task Force Vulcan," Blanche said.
"We will continue to break up narcoterrorist finance networks, prosecute violent criminals, and keep American neighborhoods safe."
Aguirre faces four conspiracy counts involving bank fraud, bank burglary and computer fraud, money laundering and providing material support to terrorists.
The bank fraud conspiracy charge carries the highest maximum penalty at 30 years in prison, according to DOJ.

title: Inside explosive Cornell rape allegations: 7 men accused, conflicting accounts and a political firestorm
summary: Seven former Cornell University Chi Phi brothers face a lawsuit alleging they drugged and raped a woman, and Gov. Kathy Hochul appointed a prosecutor.
story: Fox News legal contributor Donna Rotunno discusses what's most likely to come next in the Cornell sexual assault allegations on 'The Story.'
A sexually charged case that roiled Cornell University two years ago has exploded onto the national stage, fueling a fierce debate over sex, consent and criminality in college hookup culture.

Seven former Chi Phi fraternity brothers are accused in a lawsuit of drugging and raping a female Cornell student during a night of drinking, drugs and group sex at their fraternity house in October 2024.

The accuser, identified in court papers by the pseudonym Jane Doe, alleges the men sexually assaulted her after she arrived intoxicated and was pressured into taking ketamine and other substances. The men have denied wrongdoing, with some maintaining the sexual activity was consensual and others denying they participated in it. No criminal charges have been filed against the seven men.
CONVICTED RAPIST WHO PREYED ON WOMEN AT AMERICA'S TOP PARTY SCHOOL FACES RECKONING AFTER COURTHOUSE DASH

The case has now erupted into a political and legal firestorm, with New York Attorney General Letitia James announcing Friday that her office is conducting an "active criminal investigation" after Gov. Kathy Hochul appointed the Office of the Attorney General as special prosecutor. Cornell has separately agreed to retain outside counsel to conduct an independent review of the university's handling of the allegations.

At the center of the controversy are sharply conflicting accounts of what happened that night, including differences between what Doe said in the weeks afterward, what prosecutors say they received from Cornell police and the explosive allegations contained in a lawsuit filed nearly two years later.

The Chi Phi fraternity house at Cornell University, left, and New York Gov. Kathy Hochul with Attorney General Letitia James, right. James has opened an active criminal investigation into sexual assault allegations stemming from an October 2024 incident at the fraternity house. (Spencer Platt/Getty Images)

Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten, who initially declined to pursue charges, has said Doe's November 2024 sworn statement did not allege that she was drugged against her will or gang raped and instead described her participation in drug use and sexual conduct as "voluntary, conscious, and consensual."
Doe was 20 years old and a Cornell undergraduate when the events at the center of the case unfolded on the night of Oct. 19, 2024.

According to her lawsuit, Doe began the evening drinking vodka at her Tri Delta sorority house before attending a sorority social event at a downtown Ithaca bar. She later went to a second bar before leaving alone around 11 p.m. and walking to the Chi Phi fraternity house to meet a friend who was a member.
By the time she arrived at Chi Phi, Doe was visibly intoxicated and had consumed roughly 10 standard drinks over three hours, according to her own complaint.

Once inside, Doe alleges, a fraternity member gave her another beer before proposing a threesome with another fraternity brother. The lawsuit maintains that Doe was already too intoxicated to consent.

Doe alleges she was then taken upstairs, where two fraternity members pressured her into snorting what they said was ketamine, a drug she says she had never previously taken. She alleges they also gave her marijuana and high-proof liquor before engaging in sexual acts with her without her consent.

The lawsuit alleges other fraternity members entered the room as the night progressed. At 1:42 a.m., according to a screenshot reproduced in the complaint, one member posted "free p----" in a Snapchat group for active Chi Phi members. The complaint alleges the message encouraged other members to go upstairs.

CBS News reported Friday that it had obtained additional Snapchat messages from the fraternity group, including a photograph of Doe with another man that was shared with dozens of Chi Phi members that night. Just before the photo was posted, one participant wrote, "Like you can walk in and whip it out," while another subsequently asked, "Shop still open?" and received the reply, "Yeah."

Cornell University in Ithaca, N.Y., is facing renewed scrutiny over its handling of sexual assault allegations stemming from an October 2024 incident at the Chi Phi fraternity house. (TW Farlow/Getty Images)

Attorneys for several of the accused men have denied criminal wrongdoing by their clients. An attorney for one of the men told NBC News the lawsuit was "intentionally dishonest" and maintained his client had engaged in immature and inappropriate Snapchat messages but committed no crime. An attorney for another said the public narrative was "incomplete" and inconsistent with evidence developed during Cornell's investigation, including Doe's own statements.

Doe alleges she became increasingly impaired and eventually "completely incapacitated" as the encounters continued. The complaint says the final alleged assault ended around 5:45 a.m., when Doe lost consciousness.

Contemporaneous texts, interviews and university records show Doe described different portions of the encounter differently in the days and weeks that followed, while also expressing distress about what had happened.

When she returned to her sorority house around 11:15 a.m. on Oct. 20, Doe told her roommates she had taken ketamine and had sex with multiple men, according to records from Cornell's Title IX proceedings obtained by The New York Times. One roommate said Doe did not initially describe what happened as rape or sexual assault, while another recalled that she appeared to be "in shock" and did not seem to understand the gravity of what she was recounting.

The following day, one of the men Doe would later accuse apologized to her for how the night unfolded, saying he felt terrible that he and another fraternity member had been too intoxicated to stop things before they got "way out of hand," according to text messages reviewed by the Times.
Doe responded that "none of the sexual stuff was illegal" and said she had enjoyed being with the two men.

Other contemporaneous evidence suggests Doe was already struggling with the encounter. On Oct. 22, she visited Cornell Health seeking treatment for a urinary tract infection and testing for sexually transmitted diseases, telling a doctor she had contracted the infection "in a traumatic way," according to university records.

Doe also became increasingly distressed as word of the encounter spread around campus. A roommate told Cornell investigators that Doe initially described it as a "crazy thing that she had done," but that her understanding shifted over the following days. The roommate said she discussed portions of the encounter with Doe and told her that some of what she described could constitute rape.
Cornell University (Bing Guan/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

About a week after the encounter, Doe discovered an anonymous online post claiming Chi Phi members had been "gang banging" and that a sophomore had been gang raped. Doe later told Cornell investigators that seeing the post marked a turning point in how she viewed the night.
"That's the first time I had ever heard the narrative change that I wasn't a whore and that I was assaulted," she said, according to the university records obtained by the Times.

Doe nevertheless remained in contact with fraternity members and planned to attend Chi Phi's Halloween party, according to the records. After initially being told she was welcome, the fraternity's president uninvited her, prompting Doe to accuse the men of "covering your asses."

By Nov. 3, however, Doe was explicitly describing most of the encounter as nonconsensual. In a text reviewed by the Times, she wrote that "90% of what happened that night was not consensual," adding that she had been given more ketamine than she could remember and had felt uncomfortable around people she did not know. Four days later, she went to an Ithaca emergency room and requested a rape kit.

Doe was interviewed by Cornell University Police on Nov. 14 and Nov. 15. A transcript obtained by CBS New York shows that she distinguished the initial sexual encounter, which she said she had been "pretty OK with," from what she said happened later in the night.

"I can say with 100% confidence I was raped," Doe told investigators, according to the transcript. She also described later sexual activity as coercive and said she had been "completely and totally incapacitated."

During those interviews, the campus police investigator prepared a six-page written statement that Doe reviewed and signed. That document — rather than the complete interview transcript — was what Van Houten says his office received before deciding not to pursue charges.

According to Van Houten's account of the signed statement, Doe said she agreed to the initial threesome out of attraction and "drunken curiousness," was "pretty ok" with it and voluntarily took ketamine later in the night.

The district attorney said multiple prosecutors and investigators reviewed the statement, assumed Doe's account was true and concluded that the facts contained in it did not establish a crime under New York law. Van Houten said her credibility was "never in question."
When CBS presented the full transcript to Van Houten this week, he said it had never been provided to him.
"That wasn't information that I had," he said, later adding that its existence "changes the landscape for me."
For nearly two years after the alleged encounter, no criminal charges were filed against any of the men.

The case burst into the national spotlight Sept. 16, when Doe filed a sweeping 101-page lawsuit in New York Supreme Court laying out in graphic detail her allegations about what happened inside the Chi Phi house.
The lawsuit accuses the seven former fraternity members of sexual assault and rape and seeks compensatory and punitive damages. But it casts a far wider net than the seven men.

Doe also sued Cornell University, Chi Phi and affiliated entities, her own Tri Delta sorority and Moonies Bar & Nightclub, among others, alleging that institutions around her failed to protect her before, during and after the events of that night.

The complaint alleges Doe had already become intoxicated while drinking at the Tri Delta house before a sorority housemother accompanied her to Moonies. There, according to the lawsuit, a bouncer marked both of the then-20-year-old's hands with an "X" signifying she was under 21, but she was nevertheless served alcohol.

The graphic allegations prompted immediate questions about why no one had been prosecuted in 2024. Van Houten said he first learned of the lawsuit on Sept. 18, two days after it was filed, and that his office was subsequently inundated with calls and emails, including threats, demanding answers.

Van Houten publicly defended his original decision. He also reopened the investigation, met with Doe and her attorneys and announced plans to put the matter before a Tompkins County grand jury so it could consider her testimony and any new evidence raised by the lawsuit.

The controversy intensified after CBS reported that Van Houten had never received the full transcript of Doe's November 2024 interview with Cornell University Police. Van Houten said that if relevant information had been omitted from the signed statement provided to prosecutors, the circumstances should be investigated by someone outside Cornell.

Cornell has separately agreed to retain outside counsel to conduct an independent investigation into the university's handling of the allegations, according to Hochul. That review is distinct from the criminal investigation now being led by James' office.

Cornell, meanwhile, reached its own conclusions through the university's disciplinary process. University President Michael Kotlikoff said two of the accused students were expelled, two were suspended for at least two semesters, one had graduated before discipline could be imposed and two were found not responsible for sexual misconduct.
Those university findings were reached through Cornell's disciplinary process, which is separate from the criminal justice system and applies different standards and procedures.

Cornell has rejected allegations that it imposed only minor consequences, saying its Title IX process resulted in expulsions and suspensions. The university said no student was offered the opportunity to write essays as the sole consequence for their involvement and called suggestions that it failed to impose consequential punishment "false."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

New York Gov. Kathy Hochul and New York Attorney General Letitia James attend a news conference regarding an investigation into alleged sexual assault at Cornell University in New York City Oct. 2, 2026. (Reuters/Jeenah Moon)

Cornell said in a statement to Fox News it "fully support[s] the appointment of a special prosecutor" and is committed to "an independent external review of all aspects of how Cornell has handled this case."

The case has also drawn renewed attention to Cornell's campus climate after more than 35% of female undergraduates responding to a 2025 university survey reported experiencing nonconsensual sexual contact involving force, threats or incapacitation, up from 23% in 2023. Although Cornell said 926 of 6,000 students invited to take the survey responded, a participation rate of about 15%.
Gov. Kathy Hochul intervened Thursday, signing an executive order appointing the Office of the Attorney General as special prosecutor in the case.
James said her office would lead an investigation guided by "the facts and the law."

title: Death row inmate unconscious on ventilator after botched execution for teen’s killing: attorneys
summary: Christa Pike remains unconscious on a ventilator after Tennessee's botched lethal injection as attorneys file to preserve execution evidence.
story: Fox News senior medical analyst Dr. Marc Siegel has the latest on the lethal injection process on 'The Story.'

A Tennessee death row inmate remained unconscious on a ventilator Friday after surviving the state's failed attempt to execute her this week, and her attorneys accused prison officials of ignoring months of warnings that the lethal injection could go catastrophically wrong.

Christa Pike was scheduled to be executed for the 1995 torture killing of 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer. She would have become the first woman executed in Tennessee in more than 200 years before Wednesday night's execution attempt failed.

Pike's attorneys filed an emergency motion in Davidson County Chancery Court seeking an order requiring the Tennessee Department of Correction to preserve evidence related to what they described as the state's "botched attempted execution."
They argue the records are critical to determining what happened, protecting Pike's legal rights and ensuring accountability.
DEATH ROW INMATE TONY CARRUTHERS WON'T FACE EXECUTION FOR AT LEAST A YEAR AFTER IV LINE FAILURE IN TENNESSEE
Christa Gail Pike was scheduled to be executed Sept. 30. (Tennessee Department of Correction via AP)

"Christa remains critically ill and is receiving medical care for the devastating effects of Wednesday night's events," attorneys Stephen Ferrell and Luke Ihnen said in a statement Friday. "As detailed in today's filing, Christa remains hospitalized following Wednesday night's failed execution attempt.

"She is critically ill, unconscious, intubated and receiving breathing assistance through a ventilator," they added. "She is being treated for the serious effects of the pentobarbital administered during the execution attempt, including significant injuries to both arms."
MULTIPLE DEATH SENTENCES IN DIFFERENT STATES ARE SET TO BE CARRIED OUT WITHIN 24 HOURS: 'NOT VERY COMMON'
The emergency motion paints a far more detailed picture of what Pike's attorneys say unfolded inside the execution chamber.
Pike’s team contends the execution team struggled to establish IV access, using at least seven needles before administering two lethal doses of pentobarbital.

title: FBI overhauls tech backbone to counter AI threats from foreign adversaries, reduce response times, Patel says
summary: Kash Patel says the FBI has surpassed 140 AI use cases after inheriting decades of outdated tech held together by leadership's Band-Aid fixes.
story: FBI Director Kash Patel details how integrating AI as a human supplement allows the bureau to instantly analyze incoming public tips and intercept major safety threats before they happen.

The FBI has adapted itself and its cybersecurity capabilities to combat nefarious uses of artificial intelligence from adversarial nations like China and Russia through full-scale modernization, something past leadership relied on temporary fixes to do, FBI Director Kash Patel said.
The agency had to completely overhaul its outdated technological backbone, Patel told Fox News Digital.

"Everybody that looks at the bureau thinks they must have the best tech and technology in the world," Patel said. "We didn't because prior leadership, all they did for decades was put a Band-Aid over a Band-Aid over a Band-Aid and never took the time to fix it."
BEYOND KILLER ROBOTS: CHINA'S REAL AI THREAT TO AMERICA IS ALREADY HERE, EXPERTS WARN
FBI Director Kash Patel said the agency has harnessed artificial intelligence for use as a human supplement rather than a replacement. (Getty Images)
The FBI also harnesses the use of AI.

To handle threats with the necessary speed and scale, Patel said the FBI uses AI to scan databases and swiftly process tips from the public. The technology serves as a human supplement rather than a replacement, which dramatically improves response times for thwarting terrorist plots and school shootings, he added.

"We get tips from our private sector partners and American citizens, and those tips come into our database now finally," Patel said. "Instead of an old game of telephone, where 50 people have to call 50 people, and it takes three days to get us the information, it's ingested immediately. It's analyzed."

In this photo illustration, the FBI logo appears on a smartphone with an artificial intelligence chip and symbol in the background. (Budrul Chukrut/SOPA Images/LightRocket via Getty Images)
The leads are then sent out to field offices, FBI headquarters in Washington, D.C. is notified and personnel are dispatched to handle the issues, Patel said.
When Patel took the helm of the agency, the FBI had only two or three test use cases for AI in its entire history. The agency has now surpassed its 140th AI use case, he said.
KASH PATEL DEFENDS FBI'S ‘MOST WANTED’ BUSTS AMID MANIPULATION ACCUSATIONS, HIGHLIGHTS 'SUMMER HEAT' SUCCESS
Declaring that AI "is here to stay" at the FBI, Patel emphasized that the agency will continue to follow the law, maintain legal guardrails and partner with the private sector.

AI has come under scrutiny in recent months as lawmakers try to figure out how to regulate the emerging industry. Earlier this week, dozens of tech leaders gathered at the White House for a summit with President Donald Trump, where they signed a voluntary, "morally binding" accord focused on industry self-policing.

title: Cornell sexual assault case revives scrutiny of a little-known New York law on intoxicated victims
summary: Cornell's Chi Phi fraternity case exposes New York's voluntary intoxication loophole, prompting Kathy Hochul to appoint Letitia James as prosecutor.
story: The New York Attorney General's office is conducting an active criminal investigation authorized by Governor Hochul into allegations of a 2024 gang rape at a Cornell University fraternity house, Attorney General Letitia James announced in a Friday press conference.

A sexual assault lawsuit involving a Cornell University fraternity has thrust an often-overlooked part of New York's rape law into the spotlight, prompting renewed calls to change how the state handles cases involving intoxicated victims.

The issue gained new attention after Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten initially declined to file criminal charges stemming from allegations that a woman was sexually assaulted at a fraternity house in 2024.
Gov. Kathy Hochul has since appointed Attorney General Letitia James as special prosecutor to oversee the criminal investigation while also calling for lawmakers to revisit the state's consent laws.
MAMDANI ROASTED OVER ASSERTION THAT HIGHER NYC RAPES COME FROM 'EXPANDED DEFINITION'

The Associated Press reported the renewed focus centers on what critics have dubbed the "voluntary intoxication loophole," a provision in New York law that can make it more difficult to prosecute certain sexual assault cases involving voluntarily intoxicated victims.
Downtown Ithaca, New York in the evening. Ithaca is home to Cornell University. (iStock)
New York criminal defense attorney and former Manhattan prosecutor Mark Bederow said the debate largely turns on one legal concept: mental incapacity.

Under New York law, a person who is mentally incapacitated cannot legally consent to sexual activity. But Bederow said the statute draws an important distinction between someone who unknowingly became intoxicated and someone who voluntarily consumed alcohol or drugs.

"If somebody slipped you something like a date rape drug and it somehow severely impacted your mental capacity, but you didn't voluntarily take that, that very well would support a theory of lack of consent," Bederow told Fox News Digital. "But if you drink yourself into an oblivion, that theory of lack of consent as a matter of law would not apply."
Instead, prosecutors must rely on other legal theories, including forcible compulsion, physical helplessness or evidence the person clearly refused consent, he said.
Gov. Kathy Hochul has appointed Attorney General Letitia James as special prosecutor to oversee the criminal investigation at Cornell University. (TW Farlow/Getty Images)
That distinction has become one of the central issues in the Cornell case.
‘LOOKSMAXXING’ INFLUENCER ‘CLAVICULAR’ CHARGED AFTER TEEN ALLEGES ATTACK AT FAMILY’S CAPE COD HOME

The woman, identified only as Jane Doe in a civil lawsuit, alleges she was sexually assaulted at the university's Chi Phi fraternity house after being pressured into consuming ketamine, marijuana and alcohol before becoming incapacitated.

Van Houten said his office initially declined to pursue criminal charges because the woman's original statement to police did not indicate she became intoxicated against her will, was physically forced into sex or was unconscious during the alleged assault. He has since reopened the investigation.
FOLLOW THE FOX TRUE CRIME TEAM ON X
A man walks through the Cornell University campus on Nov. 3, 2023 in Ithaca, New York. (Matt Burkhartt/Getty Images)
Critics argue the law can leave prosecutors unable to pursue some sexual assault cases involving victims who voluntarily became intoxicated before the alleged assault.
Bederow said changing the law could force courts to grapple with whether someone truly lacked the capacity to consent or instead consented at the time and later regretted the encounter.
CONVICTED PREDATORS FACE LIFETIME BARRIER UNDER GOP LAWMAKER’S SWEEPING VICTIM PROTECTION BILL

"If you change this law, you're going to have situations where people are later asked to determine whether someone truly lacked the capacity to consent or whether they consented in the moment and later regretted it," he said.

"It’s very messy. It's tricky. There's a lot of nuance here. People need to understand how this works in real life," Bederow said.

The Cornell case has put renewed focus on what critics have dubbed the "voluntary intoxication loophole," a provision in New York law that can make it more difficult to prosecute certain sexual assault cases involving voluntarily intoxicated victims. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)
CLICK HERE FOR MORE FROM THE FOX TRUE CRIME HUB
The Cornell allegations have also renewed efforts to change the law in Albany.
SEND US A TIP

Assemblymember Jeffrey Dinowitz has been pushing legislation since 2019 that would eliminate the distinction between voluntary and involuntary intoxication when determining whether someone could legally consent to sex. Although the proposal has received support from prosecutors and victim advocates, it has repeatedly stalled.
LISTEN TO THE NEW 'CRIME & JUSTICE WITH DONNA ROTUNNO' PODCAST
Hochul has now thrown her support behind changing the law.
"Choosing to have a drink is not consent, and it's never a license for sexual assault," Hochul wrote on X. "New York law should reflect that.
"I support closing the voluntary intoxication loophole and will work with the Legislature to get it done," the governor added.

New York isn't alone. It's one of 19 states whose sexual assault laws generally treat someone as legally unable to consent because of intoxication only if they were drugged or became intoxicated without their knowledge or consent.

Some states have started changing those laws. Minnesota did so in 2021 after its Supreme Court threw out a sexual assault conviction involving a voluntarily intoxicated victim. Michigan followed in 2023, and Texas made similar changes in 2025.

New York lawmakers have tried for years to change the law, but the Cornell case has renewed momentum behind those efforts.

story: New York Attorney General Letitia James opens active criminal investigation in alleged Cornell rape

Following the press conference, Matthew Van Houten, the Tompkins County district attorney, sent the following statement to Fox News: "I support the appointment of Attorney General James and I trust that she will examine the facts and apply the law. My office will cooperate fully with the Attorney General."

Cornell University also issued a statement, saying, "We fully support the appointment of a special prosecutor and efforts to change New York State’s rape law and are committed to an independent external review of all aspects of how Cornell has handled this case."
The New York's attorney general office did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital’s requests for comment.

"According to new reports, [Jane Doe] could not have been clearer that she was 100% confident that she had been raped. Yet, shockingly, those words never made it into the account that the Cornell police sent to prosecutors," Hochul explained, citing a New York Times article. The report claimed Doe did tell Cornell police officers that she was raped, but that information did not make its way into the voluntary statement the department sent to the district attorney's office.
CONVICTED RAPIST WHO PREYED ON WOMEN AT AMERICA'S TOP PARTY SCHOOL FACES RECKONING AFTER COURTHOUSE DASH

"The attorney general then declined to pursue charges after reviewing that incomplete account and never interviewing her. Think about that. In what world would the police learn from a victim that she'd been literally gang raped while intoxicated by five men in a fraternity house, and not elevate those allegations to the district attorney? In what world does the district attorney not even interview her or anyone else involved, or even request the full transcript?" Hochul asked.

New York Governor Kathy Hochul and New York Attorney General Letitia James attend a press conference regarding an investigation into alleged sexual assault at Cornell University in New York City on October 2, 2026. (REUTERS/Jeenah Moon)
Van Houten claimed he had never been informed the statement he received was inaccurate or incomplete.

"I have never been contacted by Jane Doe’s attorneys. Not to inform me the original statement was inaccurate and not to ask me to reconsider our decision. Rather, I reached out to Jane Doe’s attorneys after the lawsuit was filed to understand the discrepancy between the original statement and the lawsuit’s allegations and the proper path forward in light of the lawsuit’s allegations," he wrote in his statement.

title: Kash Patel defends FBI's ‘Most Wanted’ busts amid manipulation accusations, highlights 'Summer Heat' success
summary: Kash Patel defends the FBI's Most Wanted list amid scrutiny, pointing to Operation Summer Heat 2.0's 8,900-plus arrests and record seizures.
story: FBI Director Kash Patel breaks down the field-centric restructuring and interagency shifts that drove record weapons and fentanyl confiscations.

FBI Director Kash Patel pushed back against critics questioning the agency's Most Wanted fugitive statistics, framing the scrutiny as an attack on rank-and-file agents while pointing to surging arrest and seizure figures in the recently completed "Operation Summer Heat 2.0" as proof of a revamped, field-centric agency.

Patel dismissed news reports that the FBI allegedly fudged its Most Wanted captures as attempts to "denigrate the work of the bureau," insisting that career staff manage the lists independently of political leadership.

In September, Patel revealed that the FBI apprehended all 10 members of the FBI's Most Wanted list during President Donald Trump's second term. On Wednesday, an MS NOW report from May resurfaced in which FBI officials said the agency has been placing fugitives on the Most Wanted list whose capture was impending.

"Look, it's really simple," Patel told Fox News Digital. "The FBI's Most Wanted list and any other campaign we're putting on has been going on for at least 75 years. The career staff at the bureau manage that list. They look and say, 'Who's the target of opportunity? Who can we get? Who's the worst perpetrator who's been on the run?' and then they announce it. I literally don't have anything to do with it."
KASH PATEL REVEALS FBI'S CAPTURE OF ALL 10 MEMBERS OF MOST WANTED FUGITIVES LIST DURING HEARING
Federal authorities said Operation Summer Heat 2.0 led to more than 8,900 arrests and the seizure of thousands of weapons and hundreds of fentanyl seizures. (FBI)

"I just think that those critics out there are super unpleased with the fact that the Trump administration and this FBI delivered on what used to be an apolitical mission of keeping law enforcement at the top and protecting our American citizens," he added.
PATEL SAYS FBI HAS CUT BUREAUCRACY, MOVED 1,000 AGENTS TO FIELD OFFICES IN 'GENERATIONAL' OVERHAUL

Patel attributed the agency's wave of high-profile arrests, record-high fentanyl seizures and weapons seized under the recently completed Operation Summer Heat 2.0 to a sweeping restructuring of the organization that permanently relocated nearly 2,000 FBI personnel to various field offices across the country and gutted Washington's bureaucracy.
The FBI, he said, has transitioned from short-term crime "surges" into a permanent, field-centric enforcement posture designed to drive down violent crime year-round.
KASH PATEL TOUTS FBI 'FULL-THROTTLE MISSION' AFTER OPERATION SPRING CLEANING YIELDS 615 INDICTMENTS/COMPLAINTS

FBI Director Kash Patel detailed the results of Operation Summer Heat 2.0, a 95-day law enforcement operation targeting street gangs, traffickers and other criminals across the country in an effort to reduce violent crime. (Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images; Graeme Sloan/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

Operation Summer Heat 2.0 was the second iteration of an operation of the same name launched in 2025 — a nationwide federal law enforcement surge targeting violent crime, street gangs and drug trafficking networks. From June through August, FBI agents, in conjunction with local authorities, went after suspected criminals in various metropolitan areas.

"You have to talk to the American people. You have to show up in the field, and you have to drive resources and permanently place people and technology in the field," Patel said. "That was the sort of overarching approach to striking at the heart of violent crime."
As a result, authorities made more than 8,900 arrests, up 3% from last summer's Summer Heat initiative.

In addition, 5,013 weapons were seized — a 120% jump compared to last year's operation — more than 1,400 children were identified or located, a 34% jump, and authorities conducted 687 fentanyl seizures, up 63%, the FBI said.
KASH PATEL TO TOUT 'LARGEST' YEAR-TO-YEAR VIOLENT CRIME DROP IN US HISTORY

FBI Director Kash Patel speaks as President Donald Trump looks on during a press conference in the Oval Office of the White House on Oct. 15, 2025, in Washington, D.C. Trump and Patel provided an update on the Trump administration's progress in reducing violent crime. (Getty Images)

"So from last year to this year, we wanted to run that playbook for Summer Heat 2.0, and the only thing we did a little differently was we added even more bodies to the field," Patel said. "So the enterprise-wide lift, shift, focus, and pivot was: we're not on defense anymore. In order to catch violent criminals and defend the homeland, you have to go on offense."
This year's operation expanded on last year's through inter-agency collaboration and other measures, Patel said, which yielded significant safety returns across urban areas.

"Just to show you that it's working in every single city and major metropolis across the country, last year for the first time, America saw 1.1 million fewer violent aggravated assaults, rapes, robberies, and homicides," Patel said. "That's 1.1 million fewer victims across the country because of what the federal government, the Bureau, and our partners were able to bring to bear across the country."

story: Gas station owner Ibrahim Aydah denies "Smax" pills found near Ole Miss student Robert Strang's body came from his store, days after a DEA raid seized his kratom stock.
FIRST ON FOX: The owner of the gas station where investigators say Robert Strang bought synthetic kratom denies that the pills found near the student's body came from his store.

Court documents show that Ole Miss students Strang, 20, and Aidan Hamilton, 18, were found dead on Sept. 21, each discovered near similar packages of synthetic kratom. Authorities said Hamilton "could have died due to a Pulmonary Edema," a conclusion consistent with a drug overdose. First responders who arrived at Strang's residence near campus found him "cold to the touch," according to dispatch audio.

A narcotics agent wrote in an affidavit that the pills found near both students were Smax Pseudo-DHM, and listed pseudoindoxyl and MGM-15(DHM) among the ingredients found on the pack near Hamilton. The Drug Enforcement Administration temporarily placed mitragynine pseudoindoxyl in Schedule I on Aug. 26, which bars its sale.

A Mississippi law enforcement agent investigating the Ole Miss students' deaths said he believes "pseudoindoxyl" refers to that compound, and lab results confirming the pills' contents are pending, court documents say.

After speaking with Strang's roommates, agents learned he had been buying "Smax" pills at Express Mart #7, a gas station in Water Valley, Mississippi, a little over 20 minutes from Ole Miss. An undercover Mississippi Bureau of Narcotics agent later bought a similar form of Smax Pseudo pills at the store. The package lists pseudoindoxyl as its ingredient, which the narcotics agent says he believes is short for mitragynine pseudoindoxyl.

Ibrahim Aydah, the owner of the gas station, told Fox News Digital he doesn't believe the "Smax" pills found near Strang came from his store. He said he doesn't put price labels on his products, while the pack near Strang had a price on it, also claiming he doesn't carry the 200 mg version.

"The package that I see on the news… it wasn't from my store," Aydah said. "The package... the Smax is 200. I never carry 200. And it has different ingredients in it than mine."

title: Lawyers, experts urge Tennessee governor to commute Christa Pike’s sentence after botched execution
summary: Christa Pike survived two doses of pentobarbital in a botched Tennessee execution, and her lawyers now urge Gov. Bill Lee to commute her death sentence.
story: Death Penalty Information Center Executive Director Robin Maher urged Tennessee Gov. Bill Lee to commute Christa Pike's sentence to life in prison after her "unprecedented" failed execution, pointing to her "torturous experience" in the execution chamber.

Christa Pike's lawyers are calling on Tennessee Gov. Bill Lee to commute her death sentence to life in prison after she remained alive following two doses of lethal injection drugs in what one death penalty expert described as an unprecedented event.

Pike, who was sentenced to death for a 1995 murder of a classmate, was rushed to a hospital Wednesday night after surviving her planned execution. Her lawyers said on Thursday that she remains in critical condition and is receiving "lifesaving medical care."
"We don’t have a sense of her prognosis or much update on her health at the moment," attorney Randy Spivey said during a news conference. "But we know she is alive right now."

The botched execution prompted Lee to halt any further efforts to carry out Pike's execution and the state’s other execution scheduled this year. He also ordered a third-party review into Pike's execution, which he called "deeply disturbing."
CHRISTA PIKE'S ATTORNEYS SAY SHE'S IN CRITICAL CONDITION AFTER BOTCHED LETHAL INJECTIONS
Christa Gail Pike is seen during her trial for the murder of Colleen A. Slemmer. (USA TODAY Network via Reuters Connect)
Pike's lawyers are now calling for her death sentence to be commuted.

Her lawyers filed an emergency motion with the Tennessee Supreme Court seeking to immediately halt and stay the execution, noting that she was in "unnecessary agony" and arguing that putting her through another attempted execution violated her right to be put to death without cruel and unusual punishment.
Death Penalty Information Center Executive Director Robin Maher, who called the failed execution "completely unprecedented," also urged the governor to commute Pike's sentence.

"Given the experience that Christa Pike went through last night, after a childhood and young adulthood that was full of gender-based violence and abuse, it would be irresponsible for state officials to put her through another attempt at execution. I really hope that in light of what she's experienced, that the governor will decide to commute her sentence to a life in prison and not put her through another torturous experience in the execution chamber," Maher told Fox News Digital.
Before the planned execution, about 25,000 people had signed a petition to Lee asking him to commute Pike's death sentence to life in prison.
An appeals court had halted her execution early on Wednesday, but the U.S. Supreme Court overturned that stay hours later to clear the way for her to be put to death.

Pike, 50, would have been the first woman executed in Tennessee in more than 200 years. She would have been the 30th person executed in the U.S. this year, driven largely by Florida's record increase in inmates put to death since 2025.
Since the Supreme Court resumed the death penalty in 1976, only 18 women have been executed in the U.S., making up about 1% of all executions in the country.

This was the second time this year that Tennessee had a failed execution. In May, Tony Carruthers, who was convicted of kidnapping and murdering three people in 1994, was not executed because officials could not find a suitable vein for an IV line, so the drugs were not administered. Multiple states have previously paused executions after cases of officials being unable to find a suitable vein for an IV line.
Christa Pike's lawyers are calling on Tennessee Gov. Bill Lee to commute her death sentence to life in prison after she survived an attempted execution. (Tennessee Department of Correction via AP)

In 2024, Tennessee switched from a three-drug series to a single drug, pentobarbital, for lethal injections. About two years earlier, the state abruptly halted the execution of Oscar Smith, who was convicted of first-degree murder, and acknowledged it had failed to ensure its lethal injection drugs had been tested properly. He was eventually put to death by lethal injection last year.
Several others have survived medical problems linked to a failure to access a vein to administer lethal injection drugs, but no one had stayed alive after receiving the drugs until Pike on Wednesday.

"This, unfortunately, is not the first time that Tennessee officials have botched an execution. There is really a quite shameful history in Tennessee of executions going wrong, although Christa Pike's really stands out. There's never been someone who has received lethal doses of execution drugs and survived until last night. This is a completely unprecedented event, even in the context of Tennessee's other botched executions," Maher said.
The Death Penalty Information Center lists 65 botched executions across the U.S. in the modern era.
In the execution chamber, Pike said she was at peace and "ready to be free."
"This is a happy day," she said.
But she remained awake, and even complained about a feeling in her arm. Witnesses reported that Pike complained of pain in her arm and remained conscious after the first dose.

An hour after officials first raised the curtains, witnesses said that a second dose of pentobarbital was administered. Pike could still be heard snoring behind a closed curtain until the microphone was cut off nearly 30 minutes later.
WHAT TO KNOW ABOUT PENTOBARBITAL AFTER DEATH ROW INMATE SURVIVES 2 LETHAL INJECTION DOSES
The botched execution prompted Tennessee Gov. Bill Lee to halt Christa Pike's execution and the state’s other execution scheduled this year. (Mark Zaleski/AP)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Pike, who was 18 at the time of the crime, and her then-17-year-old boyfriend Tadaryl Shipp, were convicted of the fatal stabbing of a classmate, 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer. Shipp was sentenced to life in prison with the possibility of parole, as he was a minor and not eligible for the death penalty.
The third defendant, then-18-year-old Shadolla Peterson, who acted as a lookout while her two friends carried out the attack, testified for the state and avoided the death penalty.

Pike did not dispute that she helped kill Slemmer, but supporters argued that her mental illness and allegations of severe sexual abuse when she was young should be considered. She was diagnosed with bipolar disorder and post-traumatic stress disorder after the killing.

"I was a mentally ill 18-year-old kid. It took me numerous years to even realize the gravity of what I’d done," she previously said. "It sickens me now to think I had the ability to commit such a crime."
The Associated Press contributed to this report.

title: France’s violent student protests raise warning for America: ‘A cautionary tale’
summary: "The Big Weekend Show" co-host says the country's violent student protests are "a cautionary tale" for the U.S., warning open borders lead to unrest and misplaced anger.
story: ‘The Big Weekend Show’ panel discusses protests in France over complaints about teacher shortages, school days and deteriorating facilities.
France’s violent student protests are fueling fresh warnings about the consequences of open-border immigration policies, with the unrest being held up as a "cautionary tale" for the U.S.
"I would also say as we’re sitting here in beautiful New York City, this is a cautionary tale," "The Big Weekend Show" co-host Tomi Lahren said Saturday.

She continued: "This is something we’re learning from Europe, and we would be wise to learn from Europe. They decided they wanted to have open borders. They decided they wanted diversity as their strength, and of course, Joe Biden tried that for four years. We’re undoing that currently."
FRANCE'S TEEN RIOTS TAKE EXPLOSIVE NEW TURN AS GOVERNMENT POINTS FINGER AT HARD LEFT
Policemen stand in front of burning garbage as they face students during a protest against under-resourced schools in Paris on Friday. (Aurelien Morissard/AP Photo)
Lahren posited that "when you let so many people come into your country, leech off of your system, then the people who are from there are going to at some point get upset."

She said that anger often becomes misplaced and, "they end up lighting things on fire, which I think is stupid no matter what you’re angry with, but it’s no doubt these countries that say we’re going to be a global home for everybody, they end up paying the price, and it’s usually the native Frenchmen, or whenever they are that end up paying the highest price."

Students in Paris began to protest late last month against what they deemed as overcrowded classrooms, teacher shortages, long school days and deteriorating conditions, blaming the government for not investing enough in education.
REPUBLICAN GLEE ERUPTS AS WHITE HOUSE BOASTS SHARP DECLINE IN IMMIGRATION FROM MUSLIM-MAJORITY NATIONS
A student kicks a tear gas canister during a protest against under-resourced schools in Paris on Friday. (Aurelien Morissard/AP Photo)

The demonstrations started peacefully in Paris’ poorer suburbs but quickly spread to Paris itself, then went nationwide in cities like Marseille, Strasbourg, Tours, Nantes, Toulouse ​and Lille, becoming increasingly violent as they expanded.

The protests were also fueled by the government’s 2027 budget unveiling on Thursday, which showed education spending would rise by only 1.7%, excluding teacher pensions, an increase which is below the rate of inflation, Reuters reported.
Rioters have committed arson, vandalism, thrown objects at police and even assaulted people in some cases, prompting authorities to respond with tear gas and rubber bullets.
TENS OF THOUSANDS FLOOD STREETS TO PROTEST SPAIN BORDER CRISIS
Students block the entrance of Voltaire high school in Paris as they protest against under-resourced schools on Friday. (Aurelien Morissard/AP Photo)
More than 5,000 protesters were arrested this week across the country, according to Reuters, and more than 400 schools remained closed as of Friday.
Euronews reported Friday that at least 65 school staff members, including 40 principals, have been injured since the unrest began, along with roughly 170 students.
More than 100 high schools have suffered what Education Minister Édouard Geffray described as "severe damage."

French intelligence agencies told a government crisis meeting Thursday that the protest movement had been initiated by politicians from the hard-left France Unbowed Party, known as LFI, Reuters reported Friday.
LIZ PEEK: ANGRY, AFFLUENT AND ADRIFT — WHAT'S DRIVING SOME YOUNG AMERICANS TO VIOLENCE

Anti-riot police officers face protesting students carrying out blockading action outside the secondary school Le Corbusier, in Aubervilliers, northern Paris on Friday. (Lou Benoist / AFP via Getty Images)
LFI has denied the allegations and accused President Emmanuel Macron's government of politicizing the protests ahead of France's 2027 presidential election.

Simone Rodan-Benzaquen, senior envoy to Europe at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies, told Fox News Digital on Thursday that the unrest began with legitimate concerns but has since evolved into something far more serious.
